utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, should we go to the closed session, please, and bring the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, I hope you can keep your promise that you have less than 40 minutes this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Please sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: We're nearing the end of our examination-in-chief. Please adhere to the guidelines that I gave you yesterday and try and focus on the main points and present your answers as concisely as possible. We left off, if I'm right, yesterday when we were talking about the events that took place on the 9th of May. I think that the last sentence we said was that you and all your family were on the floor for 36 hours without interruption, and I think I asked you what happened after those 36 hours, once you were able to get up off the floor.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the fighting stopped, an hour later, as there was no shooting for about an hour, we were able to go to the windows to look outside, and we saw that the army, the HVO soldiers, were already there. And some ten minutes later perhaps, from the last entrance of the Vranica building, which was right up next to the building of the local police of the HVO, from this entrance, we noticed about 20 civilians coming out of that building. They had a white flag, and I noticed that the white flag was being carried by Zijo Demirovic, whom I knew from before. And they moved off in the direction of the police building. But the parish, or rather, cantonal building of the police force -- I didn't see them any more after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So you saw them personally? I promised that I would just bring in witnesses who saw things at first-hand, who were eyewitnesses. So did you personally see, did you personally witness anybody expelling civilians from the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: What about the building you lived in? Were there any Muslims living there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. It was an apartment building with 21 apartments, and of those 21 tenants or families living in those apartments, 6 were Muslim, Muslim families, households, and about 9 were Croatian households, and the rest were Serbs, Serb families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, or later on, rather, did you see anybody coming into the building with similar intentions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the massacre in Doljani, at Jablanica, I can't remember what date that was exactly, but in the evening, fairly late.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether it was spring, summer, autumn?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was autumn, thereabouts, at that time of year. And it was at night. It might have been 2.00 a.m. My son woke me up - I was asleep - and he told me that three men had turned up. He even said they were drunk. He said they were drunken soldiers wearing military uniforms. And that they wanted - and let me say that at that time there were still six Muslim households, six Muslim families, living in the building. However, mostly they were elderly ladies, and -- whose sons -- some of their sons were even in the HVO army, in the HVO, or were in the municipal administration of the HVO in Mostar, and some went to visit their families, families who were in the Republic of Croatia at the time, living in Dalmatia and on the islands. And I said to my son -- I told him to invite them in. We were living on the fourth floor and they had come up to the second floor, and they wanted to expel all those six families. That's what they wanted to do, to expel those old ladies from the building. I was in my pajamas. I put on a dressing gown and went outside into the corridor. My son told them to come in, because he said that I was asking for them. One of them stayed on downstairs on the first or second floor, to keep guard, I suppose, whereas the two others came up to the fourth floor to my apartment, and to the corridor in front of my apartment. And I went to the door and said, "What do you want, guys? Why are you here at this time of night?" They didn't have any insignia, but I -- and I noticed that they were either drugged or drunken. They had pistols, and they said, "We want to evict, to, expel," that's what he they said, "the balinkusa," which means the balija women. It is a derogatory term. And I said, "Well, guys, you're not going to be able to do. They are my neighbours." That's what I said to them. And they said again, "Yes, we will, and they are not going to be neighbours of yours any longer." And we kept at it. I said they wouldn't, they said they would, and so on. So we had an argument. And one of the two seemed to become a bit more reasonable and went to the other one that was on guard downstairs on the first or second floor, while the third young man stayed on with me and we kept arguing about this. He kept telling me how that is what he had to do. And he said, "Do you know, Witness A, that the Muslims in Doljani yesterday during the night massacred an enormous number of civilians and soldiers?" And I said to him, "Listen, sir, the people that you've come to evict, to expel from their homes and expel them to the eastern side of Mostar, those people are not the ones who committed that." And they -- he said to me, "Well, they belong to them." And I said, "They might belong to them but they are not the people who did those things, and the people who did commit those crimes will be persecuted as they deserve." When they heard who I was, he left off trying to do what he was doing, but they were all standing -- remained standing in front of the entrance in the hallway of the building, and I went up to the balcony, my balcony and my window, and I was able to hear their conversation. They argued amongst themselves because they hadn't done the job they were sent to do, and I heard them say that they were going to kill me too. They said, "Well, let's kill him and then we will be able to do the job properly, the job we had come to do." So this went on for about an hour, and then I suppose they sobered up, and left. However, the next day, I informed Mate Boban that -- of the occurrences of that night, that these men had turned up, they didn't want to introduce themselves, and to prevent the same thing happening, at least in my building in future, Mate Boban issued an order to the civilian police force to place a guard in front of my apartment building. Otherwise, as a member of the presidency, even before the BH army arrived in front of my building, I had a -- I was -- security was provided for me by the police force. And the police force was again in front of my building, a security guard, and this event did not repeat itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was that done to protect you or the people in the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course, myself and all the other people living in the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber, please, if you know anything about this, were there any activities in Mostar up until the 30th of June, any activities up until the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: 1993. So from the 9th of May to the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no military operations, no military activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I meant. Thank you. Could you tell us, please, what happened after the 9th of May? Were there any peace initiatives? Did you take part in them, if there were. Could you tell the Court a little bit about that? I'm referring to Medjugorje and things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the events that took place on the 9th of May, I myself became a member of the Croatian delegation in Medjugorje on the 18th of May, 1993, along with a large delegation from Croatia, led by the President -- led by President Tudjman, and another big delegation from Sarajevo led by Alija Izetbegovic, and there was another numerous delegation made up of international representatives, amongst others Lord Owen, Stoltenberg, and as far as I remember, the President of the European Council, Larsen, and so on. So there were many delegations, and they were large delegations, all three of them, top-level ones. They discussed the implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, especially in connection with the provinces in which the military conflicts were taking place. That is to say between the BH army and the HVO. And these provinces were the Mostar province, Travnik, and Zenica, those three provinces. In the middle of these negotiations, the delegations became divided into civilian or political ones and military delegations, so the two separated. I belonged to the political, mixed delegation, and we discussed how, in these three provinces which I mentioned, to implement some sort of joint power and authority, how to secure this authority, which would prevent further conflicts between the Bosniaks and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting, but could you tell us what decisions were made, and were they adhered to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was agreed that in the Mostar province and in the Travnik province, the governor should be a Croat, and the governor Muslim, the prime minister of these two provinces should be a Muslim, and the vice-president should be a Croat, whereas in the Zenica province, the governor should be a Muslim, the vice-governor should be a Croat, and vice versa: the prime minister in the Zenica province should be a Croat and the vice-premier should be a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what was the central power to be like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The central powers needed a coordinating body as a leadership body instead of the War Presidency, because we saw the fate of the War Presidency yesterday. And to represent the Drvar people, there were three members that were put forward, nominated and appointed. They were Mate Boban, Mile Akmadzic and myself. On the Muslim side there was, in that coordinating body, Alija Izetbegovic, Fikret Abdic, and Ejub Ganic. However, unfortunately, it did not come to fruition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was the agreement signed? Did the international community approve the agreements and ratify them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. It was published. We all hoped that that unfortunate bloody war between these two nations, would come to an end. But the Muslim side did not like this, did not like it, especially as in the province of Travnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to this extent: I think there's not clarity in terms of which agreement Mr. Krsnik has just asked that was signed and approved by the international community. In the last few minutes we've talked about a number of things, and I'd like to know, please, which particular document, purporting to do what, was signed by whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe Mr. Krsnik will clear it up for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, Your Honour. I do apologise once again, because both the witness and myself are able to understand each other and follow what each other -- what we are saying in the same language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So please, Witness, you and I know what we're talking about, but could you be more specific so that everybody in the Court can understand as well, because the people here did not witness the events that we're talking about. The agreement we're talking about, where was it, who represented the international community, who signed for the Muslim side, who signed for the Croat side, where did it take place, et cetera? Could you be more specific, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that it was on the 18th of May, 1993, in Medjurgorje, which is right by Mostar. I also said that there were three delegations: the Croatian delegation, the Muslim delegation, and the international delegation. I've already said who led the Bosnia-Herzegovina delegation. That is to say, on behalf of the BH delegation, there was Mate Boban, Mile Akmadzic, and myself, and Bozo Rajic. To represent the Muslim delegation, there was Alija Izetbegovic, Fikret Abdic -- actually, Fikret Abdic wasn't there. It was Ejub Ganic. I'm sorry. Ejub Ganic. And Rusmir Mahmutcehajic, Delic. I forget his first name. He was the commander of the BH army. And on their side, there were some other generals as well, and the Minister of the Interior, Pusina. To represent the international community, I said there was -- as far as I remember, his name was Mr. Larsen. He was the president of the Council of Europe. Then there was Lord Owen, Stoltenberg, with their staff, members of their staff. I don't know those people, but they were members of the staff. But I do know the people I mentioned, and they were there. In the course of the negotiations, the military delegation, both on the Croatian side and on the Muslim side, separated. They had a separate meeting, whereas we politicians, the political delegation, had their own separate mixed meeting in order to determine these provinces. I forgot to say that from the Republic of Croatia, present at the meeting was President Tudjman, Gojko Susak, and then General Praljak. They represented the Republic of Croatia, and there were a few other individuals whom I did not know. What the military delegation was discussing, I can't say. I don't know. But I do know what the political delegation discussed, and I said that of the ten provinces, according to the Vance-Owen Plan, at least for the time being, where the greatest conflicts were taking place between the BH army and the HVO, that political and military solutions should be found there in order to bring these conflicts to an end. And the upshot was that we decided - and we signed this. We agreed and signed - that as far as the structure of power and authority is concerned, as far as the governors were concerned, governors in the Mostar and Travnik provinces, that the governor should be a Croat and the vice-governor should be a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Let me just make matters clear. You wanted to resolve the problems of the Mostar province; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Travnik, Mostar, and Zenica. Those three provinces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And you decided on the kind of government there should be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Presidency and government. The Presidency should be the coordinating body which would replace the War Presidency, at least in those three provinces, where the major conflicts were taking place between the two nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the name of the governor for the Mostar province and the vice-governor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't remember who was to have been the governor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: At the meeting, did you agree upon anything with respect to prisoners of war on both sides, anything along those lines?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the political meeting, we agreed that a mixed delegation should be set up to represent the Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather, that territory, the territory we're talking about, and that they should go and visit the Heliodrom, which is where the Muslims had been isolated, to see what the situation was like there, why it was set up in the first place. And that delegation was made up of -- representing the Croat side was myself, Dr. Franjo Gregoric, the Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia, and Bozo Rajic, who was already the Defence Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time. And on the Muslim side there was the Minister of the Interior - his name was Pusina - and Delic, the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and another general. I can't remember his name now. So all in all, three representing one side and three representing the other side. UNPROFOR's APC vehicles transported us to the Heliodrom, but before we entered the building we decided that we should mix ourselves up. That is to say that there should be three members -- that on each side, as we would not be able to inspect everyone and everything, we set up two sides again. So I was with Dr. Franjo Gregoric and the Minister of the Interior, a Muslim, Pusina, Minister Pusina. There were the three of us on one side, and then the other group made up of Rajic, the Defence Minister; Delic, the commander of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and this other general, whose name I'm afraid I've forgotten. And we entered the premises, my delegation inspected those premises, and not the other one, and vice versa. It's a well-constructed building. It used to be a military school, a military academy, for the training of aviators. And it was rather hot inside. That is to say the weather was hot in Mostar. So that these large halls had some covers, some sort of covering. But there were a lot of people there. I knew some of them from my previous contacts and from the neighbourhood. But as far as I was able to see, there were only -- the people from Mostar there were only between 10 and 15 per cent. Only 10 and 15 per cent of these people were from Mostar, and I didn't know the other ones, and I assume they had come from other places further off. So this did not last long because the people from UNPROFOR that had brought us there were in a hurry to get back. So that both these delegations met up again. That is to say we were taken back in different APCs, and when we returned to Medjugorje, the Muslim delegation joined up with the other members of its delegation, and they left once again in UNPROFOR vehicles for Sarajevo, and we stayed on in Medjugorje for dinner, for that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Was it possible for to you see the Croatian prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please tell me -- we have to hurry a bit because we have limited time, so I apologise. I'll make the questions a little shorter. Could you tell me whether, on the basis of this agreement, people were released from the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, we who went to visit the Heliodrom, we conveyed our impressions, and Mr. Tudjman asked Mate Boban to have all those who were there released as soon as possible. And there were three Muslims from my building, they were taken away, and after three or four days, two of them returned to their flats, and one of them did not return, but he preferred to go to the eastern side. I was later informed that as they were able to go to Croatia or to certain other European countries or to the eastern side of Mostar, et cetera, I was told that very soon this -- this refugee centre in the Heliodrom was disbanded, very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, at that time, when you were in Mostar, did you meet someone called Mladen Naletilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Had you ever heard of him at that time, in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: If there had been any -- if he had had a significant military or political function, would you have known about him -- should you have known about him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. At all the meetings, either of the HDZ or the HZ HB, or at other sessions, so on, whether -- whether the person in question had been -- if the person in question had been someone of importance in a political or military sense, I would have had to meet him. However, I never met him. I never saw him. It was not until the end of 1996, when he was arrested, and when the television in Zagreb started broadcasting reports about this, and there were articles in the press about this, I was a bit surprised by this because he was no one of importance at that time, at least as far as I know, at least not in my opinion. I did not know him as such. I did not know that he was an important person.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Another few questions. Are you aware of the fact that Franjo Tudjman decorated Alija Izetbegovic with the most important decoration in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm aware of this fact, and I was surprised by this. I wasn't given a decoration of any kind, and the fact that he was given a very important decoration by President Tudjman was surprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I have a little more time. I would like to ask the usher, and I want to give you the temporary number, I - [no interpretation]. When I translate this, I hope my colleagues won't object to this. Could you just confirm whether this is the rule book of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We can't talk about it now because it hasn't been translated into English. I just wanted to you confirm this. When it's translated, we shall tender it as evidence. I'm just going to ask you a question to make it possible for the Prosecutor to ask you questions about this, and this concerns the meeting when you were with Koljevic, and it concerns the presidential transcripts. You shall look through this. I'm sure the Prosecutor will ask you about this and you'll answer his questions. And my last question - and this is in the record; it's PT-3. My last question -- just trying to see how I should formulate this question, because I haven't spoken to you about this. It concerns the testimony of Mr. Kljujic, who presented things in a quite different light, things in the presidency and in political life in general. This is the last question I'm going to put to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you are talking about exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Well, he presented things in a quite different light, but I just wanted to open up this subject to make it possible for my colleagues, the Prosecution, to talk about this. When he spoke about the presidency and political life in 1992, it was in quite different terms. Likewise when he spoke about Zagreb, where you lived, apparently, you and members of the presidency.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kljujic, Stjepan Kljujic, not even in peace time, from the end of 1990 and until the beginning of the war in April, 1992, he never left Sarajevo, except in certain cases, for example as in the case of Polog on the 6th of May, 1991, and when he needed to meet up in Mostar, in Tito's villa, the so-called Tito's villa, to go out in the evening and to play cards, but never for his electorate, not even before the war, and especially not during the war, he never left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I think that my colleagues will argue about this, and my last and concluding question - and I hope I have adhered to my time limits - could the usher just briefly show you PT-3, this document? Could you have a look at it briefly and say whether what you have spoken about is really stated here in the transcripts, which we call the Presidential transcripts. You can go through it and read through it briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I said a few things about this. I said that Mr. Koljevic had presented his idea in a confused manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you didn't understand me. Do you remember -- this was a while ago, but could you read through it? Did that conversation really correspond to what is stated here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. To a large extent, it does not correspond to that. There are interjections, there are shortened sentences, there are some things that are presented as if I had said but I didn't say those things. I think that is -- is right here, in fact, where it says, "Boras Franjo." Only Koljevic could have said that. On the same page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you say which page that is on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 43 G.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: In the Croatian language; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here, on page 63, the "LJ" in the Croatian language, it's quite confused. The transcript is not very clear. When it was taken down from the audio tape, the words that were taken down, the words that I said, are not very clear. I could perhaps clarify this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: So, Witness, what I want to show with this question is that what you have had a look at, very briefly, in the few pages that I showed you when you arrived here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Don't lead on this, Mr. Krsnik. This is very relevant. Do not lead the witness on that. Ask him what he thinks about the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. I just wanted to say that because what we received from the Croatian -- in the Croatian translation, we didn't receive many pages. I didn't have the entire document. I only recently received it. That's all I'd like to say. And I won't ask him anything. I just want him to comment on this, to express his position with regard to this. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's not an objection but counsel, I hope, will accept this just for clarification so the record is clear. The words have been used, perhaps a couple of times in the last few minutes, about the Croatian translation. That may create misimpression. The Croatian, of course, is the original. It's not a translation. It is the Croatian or the B/C/S original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik, can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To confirm that? No, I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, I mean whether it is the translation of the original language of that, because there are some misunderstandings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Your Honour, I don't know where these transcripts came from. As you know we have -- haven't discussed this yet. It would be logical that the original should be in Croatia -- in Croatian, if it is the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I apologise, Witness. I just wanted to say that when we received the presidential transcripts, we only had about ten pages. When did we receive them? We received the entire transcript two days ago, and it was in the Croatian language. Prior to that we only had ten pages in the Croatian language?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm sorry, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, but I can't let that go unresponded to. The entire transcripts were provided some months ago, and I don't have -- I've not the slightest idea what Mr. Krsnik is suggesting now, but the entire B/C/S transcript was provided a long, long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't -- I have to respond to this. I received it in English. I received the entire text translated into Croatian two days ago, and I don't see where the problem is. My colleague, the Prosecutor, knows that, and all of us in the Defence, we know that too. We had ten translated pages into Croatian, and that's what I was talking about. That's what I wanted to tell you when Judge Clark interrupted me, nothing else. I don't see why we should discuss something that is evidently the truth. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear what the witness will tell us. And I have to say, Mr. Krsnik, you have passed your time limit for about ten minutes already, you know. This should never happen again. You have to organise your direct examination in a proper way. If it happens, I'll stop you, because the time limit you provided us will be regarded as the maximum time you will take in your direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this really is my last question, but you know how difficult it is to know exactly how long the examination is going to last. I think that my learned colleague the Prosecutor -- and we never objected to this, and the Defence will never object to this. We have understanding for this. We have always adhered to the time limits which were stated in the summary. We really can't be a hundred per cent precise, though, because, Your Honour, I could have put down ten hours for the examination of this witness and then I would have been quite at rest. But I didn't want to do that. I tried to be reasonable. Please accept this explanation of mine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just make two other comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, having looked at pages 12 and 14 LG very briefly, it says Witness N, that is to say, Witness A: "That's not our war, because that's not ours; it's a matter for the Serbian and Germanic people." Well, I never could have said something like that, not even in my dreams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But your name is stated there. It says that you said that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my name is stated there. But on page 13 and 14 through LG, right up at the top, it says "Nikola Koljevic." I want to say that's something that I said, to behave in a civilised manner in places where these reservists came to in particular, and what is the case in Mostar. This is something that I said within the context of the previous discussions. It's not something that Nikola Koljevic said. So I could not confirm that this is entirely identical, is a faithful translation of the conversation that we had on the 8th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions. Thank you very much. I would just like to say that I had some more material, some videotapes, et cetera, and I will just say that that's a small problem. They weren't translated and I can't show them. I'll try and find a different way to present this through other witnesses who will be speaking about the same subject, and I will use videotapes, et cetera. But now I have -- my time has been limited, and this is another problem which the Defence has, and we shall try to address these matters when we call other witnesses, incorporate these themes through other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any direct examination, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. I have three questions with regard to this transcript. Could it please remain before the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, at that time, when those discussions were held - and you have the transcript of this discussion - did you know that the discussion was being recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Afterwards, after that, did anyone ever play this recording to you or show you this transcript?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did anyone ever ask you to authorise this transcript?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness NA.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me start with some points that you made just this morning. You said a few minutes ago that you did not see any Muslim civilians being expelled on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993. Now, you said yesterday that all of the people you saw coming out of the Vranica building were in civilian clothes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw them leaving the Vranica building, and they were wearing civilian clothes and they were heading in the direction of -- they were heading towards the east from the Vranica building. I assume that they were going to the police station. That's what I assumed, because behind the building they were out of sight very rapidly, so I could no longer see them. I couldn't see where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: You said yesterday -- the only thing you've told us about that you actually saw with your own two eyes, as we say, was that all the people coming out were dressed in civilian clothes. Now, did you talk to any of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You only saw them from some distance. How far away were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, about 50 or 60 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that you have absolutely no basis whatsoever, and have not provided this Chamber with any basis whatsoever, for concluding that these men were not civilians. They were all wearing civilian clothes, you saw them from some 50 or 60 metres away, and you didn't speak to any of them; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't reply to such a question. I can't say either yes or no. Again, it would be necessary to make some introductory comments in order for me to tell you the truth. I don't know what you are insisting on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, Mr. Krsnik has told us several times that he's not going to call any witnesses who don't have first-hand knowledge of what they've testified to. Now, you've told us all you saw were men coming out of the Vranica building wearing civilian clothes, and that's the only thing you saw and the only information, first-hand information, you have, and you told us that you did not speak to any of them. And I put it to you, sir, you have no basis whatsoever for telling this Chamber, under oath, that these were all civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that after the end of the fighting around the Vranica building, I saw, about one hour later - and I saw this from my window, which is about 50 metres, at a distance of about 50 metres - I saw people leaving from the last entrance of the Vranica building, about 15 people leaving from this entrance. They were men wearing civilian clothing. The first one had a white flag, was carrying a white flag, and I saw this with my own eyes. I saw that it was Zijo Demirovic. And later on a soldier confirmed this, a soldier who was carrying a bag with documents. He entered my building and offered to give me this bag with documents which he had found in the flat of Zijo Demirovic. He wanted me to take these documents. I refused to do so. I said that it did not belong to me and that this was a matter for the military authorities, that he should hand it over to them, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir. You said that on the 18th of May, 1993, you were part of the Croatian delegation, along with President Tudjman, at Medjurgorje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Who invited you to be part of this delegation with President Franjo Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mate Boban did, the president of the HZ HB at the time and the president of the HVO. And he headed the delegation, the Croatian delegation in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was Mate Boban your boss, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what was he to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What was his relationship to you? Was he a superior in the political party? Was he a superior in some government? Was he just a personal acquaintance? What was Mate Boban's relationship to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the party is concerned, I was quite low down in the hierarchy, in the HDZ party's hierarchy. My most senior rank was as vice-president of the municipal committee of the HDZ, so that in those political terms, I was far removed from Mate Boban. As far as my participation in the Croatian delegation is concerned, I was always treated as a member of the Presidency, because I was never a member of the HZ HB or of any structures within the HVO or of any structures of the HZ HB at a later date. I remained a member of the Presidency and I carried out, to the best of my abilities, my duties, right up until the date when I was dismissed by Alija Izetbegovic in October 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to cut you off, and I mean no discourtesy, but the Chamber is concerned about time limits, and you're going off on information, I submit respectfully, that is not responsive to my question. Now, you also mentioned that Slobodan Praljak was a member of the Croatian delegation at the meetings of the 18th of May, 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And are you telling the Chamber, sir, that he was there as a delegate, as a representative, on behalf of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, at that time -- or rather, he joined the delegation, he came with the delegation of the Croatian Republic. Now, whether he was there in the capacity of a military man within the composition of the military delegation of the Croatian Republic or whether he was there in the capacity of a military HVO man, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, hadn't Mr. Praljak around that time been the Deputy Minister of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let's go back to your discussion about the presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. See if I understand your testimony. You appear to accept, do you not, that the initial functioning of the presidency, certainly after the 18th of November, 1990 elections, were legitimate, and at least during the initial phases - and we will go through this and I'll give you some dates in a moment - but at least in the initial phases, that the elections were legitimate and the functioning of the War Presidency were legitimate, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, would you agree with me that at least until the time when the war with the Serbs broke out and the two elected Serb members of the presidency, Ms. Plavsic and the other gentleman, up until the time they left, at least, you again would agree, would you not, that the presidency was a valid and legitimate, functioning body?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the other man being -- the other Serb member being Mr. Koljevic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in terms of the 1990 elections themselves, and in terms of his election as the President of the Presidency, Mr. Izetbegovic was unanimously elected President of the Presidency, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you certainly agree, don't you, sir, that the election of Stjepan Kljujic as a member of the Presidency in November 1990, that that was completely legitimate and represented the results of a democratic election, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on the 20th of December, 1991, Mr. Izetbegovic was elected to a second term, if you will, as President of the Presidency, and that in fact was with the support of the Croat members of the Presidency, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you say then that after the war, the open warfare, with the Serbs started, and Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic left the Presidency as the Serb members, that Mr. Izetbegovic was able to bring in two new Serb representatives. Can you identify for us who those two new persons were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two new persons or members of the Presidency were Mirko Pejanovic and Nenad Kecmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was certainly a reasonable thing to do, wasn't it, sir, to replace the Serb representatives who had left with two new Serb representatives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done on the basis of a provision having the force of law, which the War Presidency had already adopted. That is to say that instead of the Presidency members who in any way had left, had stepped down from the War Presidency, that the people taking their place would be those who, by virtue of the results of the elections in 1990, in November, 1990, had won the most votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, are you suggesting, sir that there was anything wrong with Mr. Kecmanovic being named as a Serb member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Viewed from this perspective, from this distance, in view of the fact that at the referendum held at the end of February and the beginning of March, 1992, had only the Croats and Muslims gone out to the referendum, in order to receive international recognition for Bosnia-Herzegovina, viewed at from this distance in time, only the members of the Croatian and Muslim people were by rights to have remained in the Presidency, in the War Presidency, but the provision that had the force of law, adopted by the President, stipulated what it did, that the elections of Mirko Pejanovic and Nenad Kecmanovic were legally all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you for a specific answer, just yes or no. Was the selection of Mr. Kecmanovic to the Presidency at that time, was that a valid action or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a valid action, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, is it also correct that when one of the Serbs resigned, they were often replaced by Croats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, when the President of the parliament, for instance, the Serb Momcilo Krajisnik, when he left the government, he was replaced by a Croat, Mariofil Ljubic; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, if I understood your testimony yesterday, you suggested that the naming of a Muslim as the head of the Territorial Defence was somehow questionable in your view. Isn't it true, sir, that as part of the War Presidency, the President of the parliament was a Croat, the man I just mentioned, the Prime Minister, Mr. Jure Pelivan, was a Croat and later Mr. Mile Akmadzic was a Croat?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Prime Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wasn't going to object but I think that it will be fair to the witness to tell him which members of the Presidency were elected and which were there by virtue of office, because the witness spent two days talking about that distinction. We have elections -- that is to say members of the Presidency that were elected there and others that were members of the Presidency by virtue of office. And that it would be proper on the part of the Prosecution and fair of him to present that to the witness in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Provide more background information when you're asking a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you told us yesterday that beyond the Presidency, the members of the Presidency, when the War Presidency was formed, the War Presidency also included a number of other senior positions, including, for instance, the President of the parliament, the Prime Minister, and essentially the head of the Territorial Defence, or what in some systems we might perhaps call the Secretary or Minister of Defence. True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only partially true. In addition to the regular members of the Presidency, and there were seven of us, in view of the fact that the Serb members had left, that is to say Biljana Plavsic and Nikola Koljevic, that left five of us regular Presidency members. During a state of war, when the Assembly is unable to meet, the regular Presidency members, according to the constitution, were to be joined by the President of the Assembly, the Prime Minister, and the commander of the Territorial Defence. In view of the fact that the President of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, had also -- had likewise left his post, then Mariofil Ljubic came to become a member of the Presidency as the vice-president of the President Momcilo Krajisnik. Jure Pelivan, who was a Croat, happened to be in a presidential function in the government, and as such was co-opted into the War Presidency. The commander of the Territorial Defence, I said, was Dragan Vukosavljevic, who the federal Secretariat of National Defence from Belgrade had appointed to that post. Not the Presidency, not even in peace time. He had already left too. So this was a free space, a free work post in the Presidency, if I can put it that way. And as the Territorial Defence did not exist as it had done in peace time beforehand - it had been dismantled; its weapons had been taken away from it - so that at that time there was no need for the commander of the Territorial Defence to become a member. That is how one should understand this, at least as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the reality is - and I'm reluctant to cut you off, to be discourteous, but I must tell you sir, and I must tell the Chamber, that I have a substantial set of questions for you, and if you give non-responsive answers, it's very unlikely that we can finish your testimony today. So I put the question to you again very simply. You objected, did you not, when a Muslim was named to the position of the head of the Territorial Defence; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that as constituted, at least up to the spring of 1992, the President -- the Presidency, the War Presidency, was well constituted with a mixture of Muslims, Serbs, Croats, and you said the replacement of the two Serbs, that you consider that a valid action, the -- Mr. Pelivan, a Croat, became a member, and it was a completely legitimate, functioning Presidency, was it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, could we stop here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll rise until quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, before we have the witness, I should say that we must finish this witness today and let him go back for the Easter holiday. So we'll reserve this courtroom this afternoon. If we do not finish this morning, we have to go on this afternoon until 7.00. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness NA, I want to make this clear to you, and in fact, clear to the Judges, that of course I am not here in any way to defend Mr. Izetbegovic, but I do want to understand fully your testimony in this regard. Sir, I put it to you that what you've told us in the last day or so is that your primary grievance, if you will, your disagreement with Mr. Izetbegovic, was simply a political one. You had some political views and Mr. Izetbegovic had different political views, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you are critical of Mr. Izetbegovic because, in your view, he was too passive in initially responding to what's often called the Serb aggression; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But sir, you certainly must understand, don't you, that in any government there are policy disagreements and political disputes; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you said that it was because of the passivity of Mr. Izetbegovic and the Bosnian government that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, or otherwise sometimes called just Herceg-Bosna, or the HZ HB -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise once again, but I have a technical detail. We're not speaking about the government, but Presidency. He was president of the Presidency, and not government. So those are two different concepts, government and Presidency, for us to be as precise as possible, technically speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. You might take into consideration the objections from Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let's just -- if we need to clarify that point, sir, let's do so, if we can, quickly. At the time that the War Presidency was formed, the War Presidency had both executive and legislative powers, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just to be clear, in light of the objection that was made, when I asked you about political disputes and policy differences, that applied to the War Presidency, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only to the War Presidency, not the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What government are you talking about, sir, separate from the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government was -- that is to say, it existed in addition to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you're saying there were no differences of political views or policy disputes in what you're describing as the government, distinct from the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were different views in the government too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very sorry to have to take the floor, but that's the same sort of question. That is something that the witness never said in this courtroom, and he seems to have been infiltrating this. So government and Presidency, can we clarify that first? Because the witness did not speak about the government during the examination-in-chief. Now, if necessary, this should be clarified: The government up until the formation of the War Presidency and the government after the formation of the War Presidency. Can we clear that matter up, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the issue of the government, I believe, is related to the Presidency, so it's quite necessary to have it cleared up. I think Mr. Scott will do that for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, contrary to counsel, I think the state of the record now, with the last several questions and answers, are in fact reasonably clear for these purposes. And it was not I who injected the issue of the government but it was on the objection of counsel. But the last answer by the witness to -- before counsel's objection was, at line 16, he agreed that there were also different views in the government too. And that's the end -- as far as I'm concerned, Mr. President, that's the end of the inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may ask him to distinguish between the Presidency and the government, to have it in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard the President's question. Tell the Chamber, please - and I ask you -- I invite to you do so briefly - the difference between the War Presidency and what you've called the government.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency, in addition to its regular functions, which were stipulated in the book of rules governing the work of the Presidency, also took over the legislative function, legislative powers, which the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina had, whereas the government was the executive organ of the Assembly and the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And while the War Presidency existed from its inception until the end, the government existed alongside it, all the time. But the Prime Minister - the President of the government, if I can put it that way - was also a member of the War Presidency by virtue of office. So the first Prime Minister who happened to be there when -- Jure Pelivan, when the war broke out, he was also a member of the War Presidency, and he remained Prime Minister with all the ministers, all those who had not left and who had not gone over to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, he was a Croat, wasn't he, Mr. Pelivan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no other questions about the government, unless the Chamber has questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you said a few moments ago, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Scott, while we are at it, may I take this opportunity to clarify something for me? Is the Presidency, which is referred to frequently in many of the witnesses' evidence, especially in the transcripts from other cases, is the Presidency the equivalent of what is the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very good question, Judge Clark. Let me put that to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: And ask where does the seat of power lie? Who is the main leader of the country?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness NA, I hope you've heard Judge Clark's observations. In your experience, in your participation in this government, all of which -- all of us appreciate the information that you can provide to us, do you use the word or concept "cabinet" when you talk about the government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talk about the government, the government in wartime, during the War Presidency, is the executive body, which is subordinate to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is the war -- is another term -- just trying to clarify and to assist Judge Clark and all of us. If we use the word "cabinet" -- would you use the word "cabinet" - and I'm sorry, I don't know if that's the exact word you would use in your language - but would you use the word "cabinet" as synonymous with the War Presidency? Or in addition to the War Presidency, was there some other executive body of what you've described as the government, which was called the cabinet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, and in practice, the practice that prevailed at the time, the War Presidency was a War Presidency, and the government, that also existed alongside, I would call that government the cabinet, although we didn't call it that in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid that the witness does not understand what the English notion of cabinet is, what the word "cabinet" means in the English language. I think that we should explain to him the concept of executive power embodied in the cabinet as it means in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I help? In western government, you have -- in a republic, you have a president who is the titular head who, but who, in effect, has no power. You then have a Prime Minister who is the leader of the political party which gains the most votes. He has the power. He is the head of the government, and he has around him his ministers with portfolios for various functions, and his ministers are called the cabinet. Now, there is a distinction between where the seat of power lies. The seat of power lies in the Prime Minister and his cabinet, and when you talk about the Presidency, what I wanted to know is where does the seat of power lie? With the Presidency or with the cabinet, who are the ministers surrounding the Prime Minister? Who is subservient to whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In our case, the seat of power is in the War Presidency. The government is subservient to the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Boras.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: One final question - and Witness NA, and I only say this -- I don't speak your language. I apologise for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have something that is just a preoccupation. Now, this answer by this witness, is it specific and applies to the situation of war only, or is this a constitutional reality of a permanent character in Bosnia-Herzegovina? That is what I'd like to find out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I have said applies to a state of war. This relationship between the government and the War Presidency, as I described it, holds true for war, times of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we just redact the surname of the witness from the text? I think it's already done. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We are in closed session. There is no need to do that. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps one just final question on this, and perhaps either you or counsel or the interpreters can assist on this. It's suggested to me that the word in the Croatian language for government and cabinet, what we might call cabinet, is the same word. I don't know. Are you in a position to say if that's true? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In times of war, during a war, the government is not the cabinet in the Western European sense of a constitutional order. But in peacetime, the regular Presidency, the regular Presidency, has all the functions -- performs all the functions that have been stipulated vis-a-vis the government, and we can say that they have parallel competencies, a kind of parallel competence and authority. So that in peacetime, the government in Bosnia-Herzegovina - and I'm talking about 1991 - the government resembles a cabinet in the western sense of power.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I think that I can be of assistance to clarify this matter up more quickly. We have -- no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. We only hear what the witness says. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm partially perhaps responsible for that, Your Honour, because I suggested that the Croatian counsel might assist us, but I understand the Chamber's ruling, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said yesterday, if I heard you correctly, that it was because essentially of the passivity - and I think, frankly, to quote you, the notorious passivity - of the Presidency under Mr. Izetbegovic, it was as a result of that passivity that the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, or HZ HB, was created as a military organisation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Not just in military terms but also in civilian terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, did you understand it to be - and I'm specifically now and very explicitly using the word "the HZ HB" and not "the HVO" - did you consider the HZ HB to be both a military organisation and a governmental organisation, or one or the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I considered it to be both.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me focus for a moment on what you say are the military aspects. You say it was created, then, if I understand you well, to provide a defence against the Serb aggression because you and others perhaps felt that Mr. Izetbegovic was not doing enough; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My question to you, sir: If it was meant to defend the aggression -- defend against the Serb aggression, why didn't the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, as you've called it, HZ HB, why didn't it provide for and take steps to defend all of Bosnia-Herzegovina against the Serb aggression?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it didn't have the military or the civilian forces to do so, because the Serbian side was helped by the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army. And as I said yesterday, it was the fourth military force in Europe in terms of strength, and that army took sides with the Serbian side. It was on the Serbian side. And it was only in parts where the Croats were in the majority, then out of the municipalities and companies, military forces were formed, gathered, to make it possible at the boundary areas, where there was a border with the Serbian side, the conflict started breaking out and they started defending areas which were inhabited by Croatian population in the majority. Because the Muslims were inert; they were passive.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, that's part of the answer, perhaps, that we're getting at, sir, but my question to you is this: Why were you interested, why was the HZ HB interested in only defending the Croat areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can't just say the Croatian areas. They also defended areas in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, wherever that was possible, wherever it was possible for the HZ HB to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why didn't you include --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostar was also defended, and in Mostar -- there were Muslims and Serbs and Croats in Mostar. And in Eastern Herzegovina -- Eastern Herzegovina was defended, and there were Serbs and Muslims there, too and Croats as well. Likewise in Central Bosnia. The HZ HB defended the entire area of Central Bosnia, where the Muslims were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you include in this the defence of the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within Sarajevo -- there were Croatian units within Sarajevo, the HVO, and together with the BH army, they defended Sarajevo from the JNA attacks and from attacks carried out by the Serbian side. This was in Sarajevo itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you've testified, I believe, based on the 1991 census, that Muslims represented approximately 44 per cent of the total population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the Croats -- the Croat population was approximately 17 1/2 per cent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in forming the HZ HB, which consisted of 36 municipalities, sir, it's true that some of the municipalities that were included in the HZ HB were not in fact Croat-majority municipalities at all, were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 36 per cent, that is to say, the 36 municipalities, as far as I know, yes, they represented the majority, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, let me give you one example. In 1991/1992, or stated differently, based on the 1991 census, Stolac was not a Croat-majority municipality, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance, I'd like the witness to be shown and distributed to the courtroom Exhibit P3.4, please. If that could be placed perhaps on the -- one on the ELMO as well. I realise everyone in the courtroom will have a copy, but some may prefer to look at the ELMO, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, what's the year of this statistics chart? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's based on the 1991 census, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to look at this Exhibit P3.4 and I'm going to ask you very specific questions to orient ourselves with this document, please, and I'd appreciate brief, responsive answers. The yellow lines, the yellow boundary that has been placed in this map of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that includes the 36 municipalities, or the municipalities, in any event, that were claimed to be part of the HZ HB, or later, the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as you just testified a moment ago, you agreed with me that in fact Stolac was not a Croat-majority municipality. And if we look at this map and to the key, you'll notice it's in this kind of a spotted green, if I can put it that way, which relates to the Muslims being below 50 per cent, but apparently being some sort of plurality, and that's why the municipality is coloured that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask if my learned colleague could say who made this map, who the author is of this map, who took the census. You will hear from our witness that various persons played around with demographic facts. This took place in Bosnia and Herzegovina. We should be told who made this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the map was prepared by the professional staff of the Office of the Prosecutor, based upon the public documents about the boundaries of Herceg-Bosna and based upon the 1991 census. If the witness disagrees with it, he can quite clearly say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one other thing, Your Honour. I don't remember that during my examination, I addressed the matter of demography and of censuses and of maps of this type, and I don't see the purpose of this questioning at the moment. Because in the list of witnesses, I said which witnesses would be appearing, and the Prosecutor could have waited for experts who would be dealing with these maps. I didn't ask the witness anything about such matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think this map is related to a question put forward by the Prosecution. We'll let him go for a while to see where he's going to lead us. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you simply just confirm to us that based on the 1991 census - and you confirmed a moment ago that the yellow line is indeed the boundaries of Herceg-Bosna - that in fact, the Croats, the Bosnian Croats, made claims upon municipalities in which there wasn't a Croat majority at all; didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I should provide an additional clarification. In all of these municipalities that you have mentioned, the HDZ had gained power.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, that's not my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in accordance with the results --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, please continue.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are issues which explain why those municipalities were within the -- came to be part of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, sir, let me just be clear. The question of the HDZ or HVO seizing power in municipalities is a separate question from demographics. My question to you was very simple. When the HZ HB proclaimed itself and announced certain boundaries, based simply on the 1991 census figures, they made claims on municipalities in which, in fact, the Croats were not a majority of the population; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't just say -- I can't just confirm that. I can't just say yes or no. With the prior explanation which I have already mentioned in brief, the HZ HB thought that these municipalities, where the Croats weren't in a majority, where they didn't have an absolute majority, they thought that on the basis of the election results in November 1990, that they had power in these municipalities. That's what the HZ HB considered to be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. We will take that for now as your answer, which I take it to mean that your answer is not that it was based on demographics but based on political power, and we'll move on and may come back to that later. Now, until May, 1992, sir, your home, if you will, and base of operations was Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My private home?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My home was always in Mostar. As a member of the Presidency, I received official premises, a small flat, and over the weekend, I would always go to Mostar to see my family, to be with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I appreciate the difference, and it may be again a language and cultural issue. I wasn't asking you so much what you considered your home town, but you were spending -- as you just told us now, you were essentially then spending the week living and working in Sarajevo, all the time that you were a member of the War Presidency, until you moved to Mostar in approximately May, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Chamber briefly what was happening in Sarajevo up until the time that you relocated to Mostar? What was happening there in connection with the fighting against the Serbs? Just remind us what was happening in Sarajevo at the time. For instance, was Sarajevo under Serb attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 4th of April, 1992, there was an all-out attack carried out. It was launched from all sides, from all places. There was chaos. Chaos resulted in the social life and the members of the Presidency. We were in the Presidency building at all times. Some people such as Mr. Kljujic and Mr. Ganic even had beds there, places to sleep, in the cellar of that building, but I lived near the Presidency building, perhaps no more than 100 metres away, so it was possible for me to go to that place where I lived after the evening sessions of the Presidency and to rest there for a while, and then I would take certain indirect routes to avoid snipers. There were no telephone lines any more, and the inhabitants of Sarajevo mounted a spontaneous resistance, and even the Serbian units came to within 200 metres from the building itself, from the Presidency building itself, and thanks to a unit which -- it was a police unit, in fact, not a military one, a unit which prevented the building of the Presidency from being infiltrated, we have this unit to thank for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, what you've told us is that during this time, Sarajevo was being shelled and there was also sniping campaign under way, wasn't there? Wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you at the time feel that the Serbs, the Serb aggressors, that you've called them, were they in any way justified in shelling and sniping at people in Sarajevo during this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was in no way justified. There was no motive to do something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were the members of Sarajevo -- the people who lived in Sarajevo, you just said a moment ago, that they rose up kind of a spontaneous defence. Were they entitled to defend themselves, in your view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you moved to Mostar in -- on the -- approximately around the 1st of May, 1992, and from that point on until -- well, approximately how long did you continue to live and operate in Mostar from 1 May, 1992 forward?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Mostar before these events in April, too. I would stay there before that. That is to say from the 1st of May, 1992, and onwards, but as a member of the Presidency, I carried out those duties from Mostar, and throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, I would also go together with the other members of the Presidency, or with certain delegations. I would even go to Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir I'm going to cut you off. I'll try not to be any more discourteous to you than I feel is necessary. My question to you is simply this: You relocated to Mostar when you went there in approximately early May, 1992. I realise you may have thereafter travelled to other places, but how long after May of 1992 did Mostar continue to be both the place that you lived and your principal base of operations? Surely you can simply tell us that lasted until 1995 or to the current time or just please tell us that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still live in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
