utterances.text: And I think you gave us the address yesterday, if I had it right. Rather than take the time for me to look at it, can you give us the address? And we are in closed session, sir. Can you give us the address where you lived both in summer of 1992 and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stjepan Radic Street, number 74, and it was on the fourth floor, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was that in West Mostar or East Mostar? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: West Mostar, right next to the so-called Vranica building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday that when you arrived in Mostar, around early May, you reported to Mate Boban. My question is why did you report to Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mate Boban was the President of the Croatian delegation on political membership, and given that on the 22nd of April, 1992, I mentioned this, I -- at the Butmir airport in Sarajevo, I had a meeting with the international delegation, with Mr. Pereiro, Cutilheiro and with Lord Carrington, and this meeting concerned Cutilheiro's plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to cut you off. That wasn't my question. I'm not asking about your meeting at the Sarajevo airport. My question to you -- and you gave a partial answer and I want to follow up on that. I asked you about why, when you arrived in Mostar in early May, 1992, why you reported to Mate Boban. It has nothing to do with the meeting at Sarajevo airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would my learned colleague please show some understanding for the age of this witness? Because he speaks very slowly. And he doesn't allow him to finish his answers. Could he be a little more patient and wait for the witness to provide an answer? He had started giving an answer. That's all I want to say. He speaks very slowly. You are well aware of this fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, you know, as a matter of fact, in almost all circumstances the answer we need is yes or no. I believe the witness is -- the witness has already answered partially the question put forward by the Prosecution, but if you want more, you may continue your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm just building on -- as the President just indicated, sir, I'm just following up on the partial answer you already gave. You said that you met with Mr. Boban, or you reported to Mr. Boban, because he was the head of the Croatian delegation -- or I want to be sure that I'm being -- yes, he was president of the Croatian delegation, on line 20. But he was not in any sense -- he was not a member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he was not a member of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So I come back to -- I'll just come back one more time to my question. Why then, on arriving in Mostar, did you report to Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 2nd of May, 1992, at around midday, I reported to Mr. Boban in order to inform him about the conversations that took place in Butmir, in Sarajevo, and to talk to him about the general situation in Western Herzegovina, that is to say in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which was under his control and about which he had information. At that time, he said, "It's very good that you have reported to me. On the 6th of May, we have to be in Graz, in Austria, to continue with talks with the Serbian side, and these talks will have to do with Cutilheiro's plan."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, sir, you just said that Mate Boban was in control, it was under his control, that is Western Herzegovina. And since Mr. Boban was not a member of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, had never been elected to any office in that government, how was it that Mr. Boban -- that Western Herzegovina was under control of Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't under the control of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina either, because the authority of the Presidency, the regular Presidency at the time, and then later on the War Presidency and the authority of the government, given that Sarajevo had been surrounded, the official government and the War Presidency didn't have any control beyond Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you continued to communicate with Sarajevo and travel to Sarajevo and, as you started to say a few moments ago, to Zagreb and Geneva and other places. You continued to carry out your functions as a member of the Presidency after you relocated to Mostar, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact, one of the means of communication you had with Sarajevo was you had -- you either had or had access to a satellite telephone, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that throughout the summer and throughout the remainder of 1992 for that matter, the Presidency, the War Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, was recognised as a legitimate and functioning government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the way that it was established, that the War Presidency had been established, but later on, with the introduction of members into the War Presidency in a non-constitutional fashion, President Alija Izetbegovic, on the basis of which international recognition was given to Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the witness to please be shown, and I'll distribute to the usher, Exhibit 136.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, this is a joint statement issued by President Tudjman, President Izetbegovic, on the 15th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I should like to -- may the witness be given the Croatian version? We've only received an English version, so the witness isn't able to read what the document is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Do you have the Croatian version?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We are not able, obviously, to translate every document overnight on a witness who appears for cross-examination. I'll ask the translation to assist us with only one relevant portion, which is paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe the original language is in Croatian rather than English; right? So you mean you don't have the original one?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I have given you, obviously, is what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Well, later on, if you are going to use some documents in your cross-examination of a witness, please be prepared with the translations, or you may inform the Court and the other party which documents you are going to use so that we could be well prepared. So today you may read the relevant part of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I feel I must respond, and with all respect, we have not been provided any documents, any exhibits by the Defence, translated or otherwise. We do not know the nature of the examination that's going to take place until the witness appears. And, Mr. President, again, with all respect, the Chamber knows of the difficulties this institution faces with translations. Now, I can just represent to the Chamber, in all good faith, we cannot be in a position always of being able to have the direct examination of the witness yesterday, identify all of the documents for cross-examination last night, and have them translated by this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at least you have to inform us which documents you are going to use during your cross-examination before you do your cross-examination. And now we are not going to debate on these procedural matters. You may --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you may proceed along with the suggestion we made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and I do appreciate the Court's patience. We'll go forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the point is, if I can ask you to look at -- and I'm only directing you there so you can visually see what I'm referring to, and I'll ask for Translation to assist. If you look at paragraph 3 -- for purposes of translation, I will simply read it out in English, Witness NA, and I'll ask you to please listen to the translation. It says: "The Republic of Croatia supports Bosnia-Herzegovina's efforts for preserving its independence and repulsing the aggression, and is giving and will continue to give aid to this end. The Republic of Croatia also supports the efforts of the legal government and the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina to consolidate the defence of the Republic by uniting all aspects and components of armed resistance into unified military forces under the command of the Presidency." Now, sir, this is a joint statement issued by not only Mr. Izetbegovic, but President Tudjman, in June 1992. And do you quarrel that that is an accurate description of events, that the Republic of Croatia recognised the Presidency as the legal government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. I agree with the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown next - and on this one I will ask for the registry's assistance please - P159. I did not bring extra copies of that. And I believe, Mr. President, there is a B/C/S version of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I believe you testified about this document yesterday. This is a copy of the 21st of July, 1992 agreement of cooperation between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia. And I hope you have there in front of you -- there is a Serbo-Croatian/Bosnian language translation for you. The first question, sir: Isn't it true again that by this document, the Republic of Croatia identified and recognised the existing government of Mr. Izetbegovic as the legal government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which document? You mean the one I've just been given?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Exhibit P159. Maybe we don't have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can I have the usher assist and look? Perhaps we don't have the right document. Can I just see -- no. I can see by looking at it, Mr. President -- maybe the numbers -- it may be completely my fault. The problem is, Your Honour, the number has been cut off. The copying has cut off most of the number on the page. Let me ask the usher to please -- this is the 159. It should be in the binders. Mr. President, to be clear, the Chamber and the Defence counsel should have in the Prosecution Exhibit binders P159. And I do have - if it is not accompanied in that document, I apologise for the apparent confusion - I do have the Bosnian-Croatian version here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I think that we should have prepared everything that was in the cross-examination, at least a list of documents or materials that we use in cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I agree with you. We have already made a ruling. We believe that for the next witness there will be some improvement. Mr. Scott, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise for the confusion on that. You have in front of you now a Serbo-Croatian version of that document, and you see, do you not, that that is a copy of the 21 July 1992 agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And my appending question to you, sir, before the difficulties with the document was: Is it correct, sir -- or isn't it correct that again in this document the Republic of Croatia recognised the government headed by Mr. Izetbegovic as the lawful government of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, the president of the Republic of Croatia recognises Bosnia-Herzegovina as a legal state. However, this particular agreement -- Alija Izetbegovic never presented this agreement before the War Presidency for the War Presidency -- never put it up for adoption before the War Presidency to adopt or not adopt. And furthermore, Alija Izetbegovic never, through his party, the SDA, he never -- the Muslim side - his voters, his sympathisers - they were never informed of this agreement, and I said a few words about that yesterday. Because I personally, as --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, forgive me, but you've gone beyond my question. If counsel -- I'm sure that if Defence counsel wants to follow up on that, they will, but you've answered my question, sir. You said: "Unfortunately the president of the Republic of Croatia recognises Bosnia-Herzegovina as a legal state." Now, why was it unfortunate that President Tudjman, in your view, recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as a legal state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because on the other side, that is to say, on the side of Alija Izetbegovic, he did not respond in like terms. Because in his Bosnia-Herzegovina and in the War Presidency, he never presented this agreement for it -- he never said that he had agreed upon this and signed it with the president of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So then, sir, it's your view that in fact this agreement was completely invalid and that to the extent that there were armed forces of the Republic of Croatia on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, that they were there illegally and as an invading force?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say that there's been a lot of interjection here, tripping up. When did anybody speak of the HV in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and did we discuss this with this witness at all? I was listening to the Croatian interpretation and I'm using my other ear to listen to the English translation, to control that interpretation as far as my English enables me. "The forces of HV which were in Bosnia-Herzegovina" is what the witness said. Now, the question should be: Were they there or not? That should be asked first, without trying to trip the witness up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. Split your question in several parts and put it very clearly to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness NA, separate from my question whether or not you believe or recognise or acknowledge the presence of HV forces in Bosnia in 1992. That's not my question at the moment. But what you're telling the Chamber now is: This agreement between the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was an invalid document that had no force and effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not have any legal worth because it was not presented by Alija Izetbegovic to be approved by the War Presidency. I consider this agreement - on the one side, by the Republic of Croatia, and on the other, as president of the SDA party, Alija Izetbegovic - it is their agreement. He would often do this, do things like this, not only in this particular case but in other instances as well. And his agreement held greater weight, as president of the SDA party, than -- as far as I recall, he never signed anything in the name of the War Presidency ever either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to just state this question to you one more time and we're going to go forward. And please, a yes or no answer. By your testimony this morning, this document had no legal force and effect, because you've told us that President Izetbegovic had no authority to sign it on behalf of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to next ask for the usher's assistance, please, in distributing to you and to the courtroom Exhibit 200.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Scott, while you're distributing those papers and while we are on the subject - because for me to ask a question a couple of hours later may make the question lose its validity - could you ask this witness whether the powers of the President during a declared war, in other words his Presidency is transferred or transformed into a War Presidency, does that President have powers to sign agreements without having to have those agreements ratified by the presidential cabinet or the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness NA, I hope you've heard the Judge's comments. I wanted to allow for translation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not even in peacetime, when the regular Presidency was functioning, did Alija Izetbegovic, as the presiding officer of the Presidency, he was only the primus inter pares, first among equals, and as an individual, in peacetime, without a meeting of the collective Presidency, could he sign anything before the collective Presidency gave its approval to what had been agreed beforehand. And this was particularly true of the War Presidency. The President of the War Presidency, and that was Alija Izetbegovic, because the War Presidency was also a collective body of men, and Alija Izetbegovic, as first among equals of that collective organ, had to have each agreement which he had agreed upon, concluded with a statesman outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, had to present it before the collective War Presidency to be discussed, and then that collective body, once it gave its approval for signature and ratified it, only then could it be signed by Alija Izetbegovic, who was still at that time the presiding officer of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: The question I asked that follows up on that is a question that my colleague Judge Diarra posed, and I thought the answer was unsatisfactory. Does this witness make no distinction between the powers of the President during a declared emergency, such as a war, and the powers of the President in peacetime? Is he saying that a president who negotiates outside the country must, before he reaches any agreement, seek ratification, in wartime as in peacetime? I find that personally a little illogical but I'm open to explanation and I think Judge Diarra had the same concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, it's obviously not my answer you're interested in, but that was the reason for my questions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, let me see if I can come at it one more time. We are talking about a War Presidency here, and you've told us in the last two days about significant powers that the War Presidency takes on that perhaps may not be in effect during more normal conditions, in peacetime conditions. Now, are you saying that the President of the War Presidency during a time of war has no ability to sign or enter into agreements with other states or other governments, to provide, for instance, assistance to the country?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we are not going to get anywhere like this because we don't understand each other. It's the same thing as with the cabinet. There is no President of state. The President of the state is not the President of the Presidency but all members of the Presidency because it is a collective body and he's a collective President and one person presides over the Presidency. So it's not the President. It's the presiding person over the Presidency. This concept doesn't exist in the west. It is a model which in our country was introduced in Yugoslavia, that is to say, because of the multi-nationality character of the country. So all seven individuals make up one President. But there is one presiding person, one presiding officer, at any given time, of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, when the counsel asks a question to the witness, we don't like the Defence counsel to answer this question instead of the witness. No matter whatever the witness said, we will take it. And Mr. Scott, your question is too complicated. Try to make it simple and understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll try. It's hard to depart from what was said by counsel and what's been said, frankly, by the witness, but I'll try to reframe it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it your understanding, sir -- what you're telling -- your testimony to this Chamber that Mr. Izetbegovic as the President of the Presidency - and elected to that position, by the way - had no authority to enter into such agreements as the one we have been looking at in the last few minutes, during a time of war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic was not the President. He was the presiding person in this collective organ that was called the War Presidency. Similarly, he was the presiding person in peacetime of the regular Presidency. I said that this presiding person of the War Presidency, he was that, compared to the other members of the War Presidency, and he was only the first among equals, primus inter pares. He presided over the meetings. He chaired the meetings. But he was not able to do anything as an individual without the collective Presidency, all the members of this collective body. He could not make any independent decisions on his own without the other members of this collective body. I don't know if I make myself clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: We'll pass on from that, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, let me come back at this series of questions in a slightly different way. I put it to you, sir, that the answers you're giving to the Chamber today are what might be considered technical answers but are not, in fact, consistent with what was actually taking place on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 and 1993, and in fact, as recognised by the President of the Republic of Croatia. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give a yes or no answer, without explaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, sir, we are going to have to move on, and I appreciate the Chamber's guidance and the Chamber can certainly have additional questions, all that it, of course, wants. I do have to move on with my examination at some point. Sir, what I have shown you this morning, and I'm showing you another document now, Exhibit 200.2, which was now distributed some minutes ago, and I put it to you, sir, that in reality -- and unfortunately, we all know in the time of a war some of the niceties may go by the board. But the international community, the Republic of Croatia by its President, Franjo Tudjman, and any numerous international organisations and bodies recognised President Izetbegovic as the President of the Presidency of the lawful government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'll take that as your answer, sir. Would you look, please, as Exhibit 200.2? And again, with my -- yes, I understand, sir. I was about to tell you -- I apologise that I cannot put a B/C/S version in front of you but with translations -- well, before I get to translation, can you tell the Chamber who was the person in December 1992, the person in position of a man named Mile Akmadzic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December, 1992, it was -- Mile Akmadzic was the Prime Minister of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He replaced the former Jure Pelivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was he a Croat or a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the clock but if I could finish this one document, it might be the time to take our recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, I'm going to direct your attention to the second page of the document, and I will ask the translation be provided to you, of course. But this is a press article dated the 9th of December, 1992, and if I can have the assistance of translation, I'll read this, but it's -- for the courtroom it is the seventh paragraph starting on page 2. Let me just double-check that again. Starting with the word "Akmadzic." Listen, please, sir to the translation. "Akmadzic said that although the Bosnian government fully supported UNPROFOR's role in Sarajevo, he believe that it was 'violating its mission' in particular cases." In the interests of time, let me then take you down -- skip two paragraphs, to the next "Akmadzic." It says: "Akmadzic said Bosnian government troops had gained the advantage in the last three days of fighting in Sarajevo but reiterated his government's plea to lift the UN arms embargo imposed on former Yugoslavia." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Now, sir, once again, I put it to you, the Croat Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina was referring here to the Bosnian government, and it was the Bosnian government that was recognised as the lawful government of Bosnia-Herzegovina in December, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the witness is being asked his opinion. He's being shown documents whose origins have not been disclosed, who wrote them, what context this is mentioned in. In this case only Mr. Akmadzic can testify, and quite certainly not Witness NA. So he ought to be told what document -- what the document is, that it is something that was written by Kevin Sullivan from Sarajevo. What organisation he belonged to, one doesn't know, probably some international community organisation. And so he is second-hand witness already. And now this witness is asked to state an opinion and to confirm something he has absolutely no idea about. Nor is he able to testify in any way whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, partially we agree with the Defence counsel that we are very suspicious about this document. The previous two documents were agreements between the governments or between the Presidents of the two countries, if I may say, but this one, it may be just a news report appeared in a newspaper. You could not use this newspaper report as a basis to establish whether the government is lawful or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, and that certainly wasn't my intention, but let me ask the question differently. I hope I can address the Chamber's concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if I represent to you - and I believe I can do so in good faith - that Mile Akmadzic, who you have identified as the Croat Prime Minister of Bosnia-Herzegovina - if I represent to you, I think in good faith, that he, as late as December, 1992, referred to the Bosnian government, did you -- would you understand him to be referring to any other governmental body than the government that was based in Sarajevo, the War Presidency of which was headed by Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer, either positive or negative, yes or no, in connection to what Mr. Mile Akmadzic said at the time, because already at the end of 1992, by the end of 1992, the War Presidency had lost its legitimacy, because of the introduction into the War Presidency of members in an unlawful, unconstitutional way. So as the War Presidency had lost its legitimacy, by the same token, the government could not be a legitimate government either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've taken the Court's time and I appreciate that. I'll end the question at that point for the break -- for the purposes of the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay. Because of other obligations of the Judges. Bring the witness, please. We'll start this afternoon at 3.00 in the same courtroom. Mr. Scott, how long are you going to take for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, noting that my time hasn't started yet this afternoon, so I haven't taken the last 15 minutes, Your Honour, I roughly predict somewhere -- the Chamber has observed the witness and the nature of his answers. If the answers were to get a bit shorter and more responsive - that's the only way I can answer the Chamber's questions - I think I might be able to do it in something around two hours or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That means we might be finished before 5.00; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, depending on all the breaks, obviously, et cetera. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you. Sit down, please, Witness. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness NA, in moving forward, I'm going to try to raise a couple of topics with you in a rather, I hope, abbreviated fashion, so I will appreciate any responsive answers you can give. You said yesterday that the Islamic declaration had been incorporated or made part of the SDA political platform, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I heard you well, you also, however, said you had never read the Islamic declaration. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I put it to you, sir, you have no way of knowing whether anything from the Islamic declaration was incorporated into the platform or not, because you don't know what's in the Islamic declaration, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me provide an explanation. I didn't read the entire Islamic declaration, but through various articles that appeared in the press, I became familiar with the Islamic declaration. And when I compared it with the SDA party's programme, I could find certain places where it was quite explicitly stated that the SDA party belonged to those of Muslim faith, religious people of the Muslim nationality, and that it drew -- its political party came from the Muslims who were of religious faith, and it said that the Muslim electors would vote for the SDA, and it is in that sense that I connect the political programme of the SDA party with the Islamic declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put my question to you again. You don't know anything about the Islamic declaration, do you? You've never read it, and if I were to show it to you today, you would have to say you're not familiar with it; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the witness has answered that question and I think that the question is being repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. The witness has already answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What you're telling the Chamber, then, sir, is that the only thing you know about the Islamic declaration is what you've read other people say about it. You said you read articles. That's the only basis of your knowledge for anything about the declaration?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I take it, sir, apart from what you've said to us already, you cannot point to any provision, section or article of the Islamic Declaration that was specifically, as you say, incorporated into the SDA political platform, can you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you made the point of telling the Judges yesterday that Mr. Izetbegovic had been imprisoned at one time for his political views based on the Islamic Declaration -- and I want to make clear, sir, that had that not been asked of you, I would not ask you the question I'm about to ask you now, but I feel now that I must. Have you, sir, ever been imprisoned because of your political views?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why were you imprisoned, sir, and by who?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army imprisoned me because I refused to be -- I was offered to remain in the army and they would have immediately given me the rank of sergeant. They wanted me to become a member of the League of Communists. I refused to become such a member. I rejected other offers or suggestions, that is. They wanted to get me as a young Croat and they had offered me the rank of lieutenant, because the Croats needed me, especially the Croats from western Herzegovina which is where I come from originally. And in fact, I had been put on trial for political reasons. But when I refused all of this, then I was put on trial for abuse of my duties, of my responsibilities, in a certain military company, where I had been employed. And they wanted --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me take you, sir, to the first trial you just mentioned. You were apparently making reference to two trials. You said you were initially put on trial for political reasons, and what was the basis of that trial? What political reasons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, yes? You want to make an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I want to object, Your Honour, because the witness did not speak about two trials. He was just saying that -- he was just telling us what had happened to him, and I think that once again, words are being put into his mouth. These are things that he did not say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, this question will all depend on the witness would like to answer it or not. Let us hear the witness first, whether he would like to answer it or not. If he refused, we will believe that there is no reason for asking this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the -- what I wanted to ask with my question, but it's not relevant. My colleague can conduct his cross-examination as he wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I say something, Mr. Krsnik? You've interrupted and objected at least 20 times, I think. It's very unusual for counsel to interrupt a cross-examination except for very strong reasons. It's very difficult for the Trial Chamber to get an impression of what the witness thinks under pressure if you keep jumping in. So unless the objections are really very pertinent, maybe we could try and get a free flow. I know that there are occasions where you feel it's absolutely necessary, but try to minimise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am only behaving in the same way that people behaved towards me when I had a cross-examination, when I was standing here in the helpless manner and there were objections coming to me from all sides. And as you can see, I am trying to restrain myself. I am making a big effort, and especially there were objections about criminal responsibility. But these questions, they don't bother me. I just want them to be put correctly. That is the purpose of my objections. And I think that it is quite important. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, I've got a question to ask you. Are you going to answer the question put forward by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which one? Could you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, you may repeat your question, the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, there was some confusion about the last question and now I don't know if I can go back to it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: That's about the first trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, I must say I disagree completely with what Mr. Krsnik said earlier. The witness specifically made reference to there was a first trial and then he went on to say there was a second trial. In the first trial, he said it was something about his political views.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So my question to you, Witness, is: What was the basis of the first trial against you that you say was based on your political views? What were you accused of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was only one trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Witness. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the trial was for the abuse of official power, but that was at the time of communism, such as it was, but the background was political. When I -- when before the trial for abuse of power, when the JNA offered me the possibility of becoming an officer of theirs, and the possibility of becoming a member of the League of Communists, when I was offered the possibility of taking -- of leading youth brigades to construct rail track at the time, when I refused all of these offers, then I was set up in the military company where I was employed. First of all, I was given the authority to --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to cut you off. And I'm only going to ask you this question only one time, and then I promise the Chamber and you, sir, that I will move on. I'm going to ask the question very bluntly now because I've tried to come around it in a more delicate way. Sir, you were imprisoned because you fought on the side of the Nazis during World War II; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I said I'd move on. I will. In terms of the constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, sir, you were in Mostar in September 1992 when the constitutional court's decision declaring Herceg-Bosna illegal was announced, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in Mostar at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when, in fact, did you first hear of the announcement or the ruling, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite late. It was three or four years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Three or four years later? Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said yesterday, I believe, in your testimony, that at that time, you attacked the legitimacy or the validity of that ruling by saying there were only Muslims on the Court. Sir, wasn't Pero Krijan on the court at that time, as reflected on the court's decision? And he was a Croat, was he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I heard about that decision, about three or -- three years or more later, then the people who informed me of this told me that at that time, when that constitutional decision was adopted, I was told that not a single member of the constitutional court was a Croat or a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, again, Mr. President, I have to say, my estimate of two hours is based on getting responsive answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question to you. Pero Krijan was a Croat member of the Constitutional Court in September of 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Pero Krijan was a Croat and whether he was in the Constitutional Court at the time that decision was adopted. Pero Krijan need not be a Croat. Perhaps he was of some other nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Dr. Nedzo Milosevic was a Serb member of the Constitutional Court in September 1992, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names. I don't know the composition of the Constitutional Court in terms of the names of its members. I was only able to hear from others that there were no Croats and that there were no Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So what you've told the Chamber, sir, is completely based on what you heard someone else tell you three or four years after the fact, and other than that, you have no basis for telling this Chamber yesterday that the court was not functioning at the time; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that at that time there were no representatives in the Constitutional Court who -- that the Serbs and Croats weren't represented in the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you're not listening to my question again. Please listen to my question. The only basis you have for saying that is what someone told you three or four years after the decision was announced, and in fact, you have no first-hand knowledge of the make-up or functioning of the court in September 1992, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I have no first-hand knowledge of the manner in which the Constitutional Court functioned at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you said yesterday that you learned of some evidence or information that the Muslim forces -- I'm going to use that term to avoid quarrelling with you about whether it was Territorial Defence or the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, so let me just say "the Muslim armed forces." You said that you had information that the Muslim armed forces are the ones who attacked, who initiated the fighting in Mostar or around Mostar on the 9th of May, 1993. Now, is that your position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, again, Mr. Krsnik is telling us that he's not going to ask you anything that you don't have first-hand knowledge of. What first-hand knowledge do you have that that's true, the basis of your assertion to that effect?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I said, and today I can repeat this: Around the building in which I lived and where I still live today, the BH army, not to say the Muslim army, was making military fortifications, defence positions, not just around my building but in the entire area, and even around the well-known Vranica building, where very intense fighting was going on. And that is my first-hand knowledge. And especially on the 9th of May - that was a Sunday - at about 3.00, I heard BH army soldiers who were in the catering establishment in the basement - and I lived on the fourth floor - I heard them singing and making a lot of noise and so on. But at about 2.00 or half past 2.00, they received the order to go to their positions. I was awake all that time, for five hours. At 5.13, shooting started from light weapons, and later on they used large-calibre weapons and so on. That is the first-hand information that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I was going to say, I'm not going to prevent you from giving your full answer, but just to move us on: Your answer is you based that on having heard these comments by these ABiH soldiers somewhere near your flat on the night between the 8th and 9th of May; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was already the morning of the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And do you have any other basis, apart from that, which we understand. You've clarified that. But do you have any other basis for telling this Chamber that it was the Muslims who started the fighting on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about that yesterday too. In two months or three months, the HVO left the Vranica building and left it to the BH army, and in a month or two there were military fortifications. They had placed sandbags around the Vranica building. This is what the BH army did. I went to see Arif Pasalic then --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there, then, not because I'm disagreeing with you. The second reason you're telling us is because you saw the ABiH building -- or adding fortifications to the Vranica building; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me -- on both of those matters, you've gone to some length in being very critical of the Muslims for previously being, in your terms, too passive in terms of the military preparation. Now, are you suggesting that the Muslims were not entitled to have armed forces or fortifications in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, as far as I know -- I wasn't a military person, but from the contacts that I had, at the beginning, the following were part of the HVO: There were Muslims who were part of the HVO, and as far as I know, Jaganjac -- I don't know his first name, but he is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise, but again, respectfully, we're now talking about Mr. Jaganjac and something that happened years earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir: Do you agree that the HVO forces had armed forces and fortifications in Mostar in April, May 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Both the BH army and the HVO had forces -- had fortifications. I think that in Mostar, the BH army had a greater area under it. It had more territory than the HVO. The Vranica building itself is in West Mostar, as is my building, the building where I live, and the BH army controlled Mostar up until that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, we've now established that both the Muslim side and the HVO had armed forces and fortifications in Mostar in April and May 1993. Now, are you telling this Chamber -- correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you telling this Chamber that the HVO was entitled to have forces and fortifications in Mostar but the Muslims were not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I want to say. That's not correct. The Muslims had just as much -- the BH army had just as much right to do this as the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to put it to you very clearly that every neutral observer, including the witnesses that this Chamber has heard, including the UNPROFOR, including ECMM, including a humanitarian organisation whose name I cannot mention, but the Chamber will recall the witness, protected witness, all of those close observers of these events, not Muslims, not Croats, have all concluded that it was the HVO who attacked Mostar on the 9th and 10th of May, 1993, and that's true, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell me, sir: How many Croat women and children -- on the 9th and 10th of May, how many Croat women and children were taken to the football pitches and put on buses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, just so you know, I'm making efforts. I've just skipped over several pages of my outline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to take you back to Miro Lasic. He was one of these persons, a Croat who was named to the Presidency after the 1990 elections, that you identified yesterday, and you said putting Mr. Lasic in the Presidency was another unconstitutional act. But you also then testified, I believe, that Mate Boban approved putting Mr. Lasic in the Presidency. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that Miro Lasic was -- entered the War Presidency in an unconstitutional way, but I don't know how he came. I can simply assume that it was because of an agreement between Mate Boban and Alija Izetbegovic. This is something that I can just assume, because without the consent of Alija Izetbegovic, as the presiding person in the Presidency, in the War Presidency, and without Mate Boban, who was a political functionary and the President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, I know that this could not have happened without an agreement between the two of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So this wasn't a situation that you've told us about in other instances where you accused Mr. Izetbegovic of taking some unilateral action, but according -- at least as far as you know, this is something that Mate Boban approved; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was approved, but Mate Boban could not have approved of this. The presiding person, Alija Izetbegovic, he could only present this proposal to the War Presidency, and then the War Presidency should discuss the matter and take a decision as to whether Miro Lasic, as a Croat who was not a candidate for a member of the Presidency and wasn't a representative in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina either, they should then take a decision as to whether he could enter the War Presidency. The War Presidency would certainly have rejected such a proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Then what you're telling the Chamber is whether or not Mate Boban had approved it would not take make it any more constitutional or proper one way or the other? The fact is if Mr. Boban had said, "I approve this," you're telling us it was still not a valid or a proper thing to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Boban had no legal authority or say-so as to who should be a member of the Presidency of BIH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You say that the two Serbs who joined the Presidency after Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic resigned in the first quarter of 1992, that they were replaced by these two other Serb members. I believe, sir, you've said that these two Serb members were paid. Have you ever said that they were paid by Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand the question. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, have you ever taken the position -- have you ever told anyone that these two Serb members were paid by Izetbegovic to be members of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two members, those two Serbian members, who replaced Biljana Plavsic and this person Koljevic, they -- on the basis of a decision rendered by the War Presidency, on the basis of a legally valid decision, given that in accordance with the results of the elections of November 1990, they were those who had obtained the greatest number, they were the next ones who had obtained the greatest number of votes, according to that decree issued by the Presidency, they automatically became members of the War Presidency. At that time, we were all paid from the treasury, by the treasury of the Presidency, let's say the treasury of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that what you meant -- let me just try to move this on, sir. Is that what you meant -- if you said that they were paid -- let's just take it one step at a time. Are you suggesting that they were simply paid by the government -- try to use a neutral term --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm really trying to be patient. This witness never said that anyone was paid, in particular, but this is the 15th time that he's explaining this, from when I started asking him questions, and now that the Prosecution is asking him questions, he has been explaining how members of the Presidency received their salaries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, from the answer of this witness, it's quite clear, those members of the Presidency were paid by the treasury of the War Presidency. I think that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I only then have one follow-up question and I appreciate what you just said. And that was -- I had come to exactly the same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So sir, you were not suggesting before - just giving you a chance to explain this - to the extent you had accused these people of being paid, you weren't suggesting that they were being bribed by Mr. Izetbegovic, were you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must understand the situation. A regular salary for members of the Presidency, the War Presidency, my salary too, included, from the 1st of May, 1992, up until Alija Izetbegovic dismissed me in October, 1993, the monthly salary was two German marks. It was the equivalent of two German marks. That was the salary according to the calculations in 1995 when I came to pick up my employment booklet in order to regulate my pension and retirement. However, the members of the Presidency who supported Alija Izetbegovic in his positions and policies and his political options received an additional sum of money from the treasury of the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA party. I know about that because when we met, that is to say the War Presidency, when we met in Zagreb, in the building of the embassy of Bosnia-Herzegovina, on that occasion, we would be given our travel expenses, per diems, our hospital -- hotel, I'm sorry, hotel expenses, and the ambassador of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was a lady, her name was -- what was her name? Can't remember now. But she told us that the Croatian members should go home as soon as possible in order to travel on to Geneva at the invitation of Lord Owen and Stoltenberg, that the War Presidency was to continue its meeting over there, and Biserka, that was her first name, the ambassador's first name was Biserka, she said that we should be patient, for the money from the treasury -- Presidency, from the treasury of the SDA to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can have the usher's assistance, please, to put this in front of the witness, please? Counsel -- I direct counsel's attention to the statement of this witness dated the -- signed by him on the 10th of December, 1996. I'm looking at the last page of the English version, counsel, on page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember giving an interview statement to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor in the -- November and December, 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention, please, to -- I have handed you the B/C/S version, if you will look toward the end of that document, about three paragraphs up from the bottom, from the very end of the statement, you skip up, please, three paragraphs, you'll find a paragraph - I'll assist you as much as I can - it's a paragraph that -- it's a long paragraph. The first few words of that paragraph start, "The work of the Presidency." Can you find that paragraph, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't. I can't find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Please go up, several paragraphs from the end of the statement, probably either the last page or next to the last page, could you please find that begins with the words, "The work of the Presidency"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a paragraph beginning, "Statute." Could you please start reading it out and then I can check to see whether this is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to take you straight to it, sir, then I'm going to give you every opportunity to find it. You said at that time, did you not, that the new members were Serbs from Sarajevo and were paid by Izetbegovic and through their bias, Izetbegovic used the Presidency to promote his pro-Muslim policy? Is that what you said in your statement in 1996?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Page 11 of the English version, counsel. I'll try to find -- I think it might be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've been looking for it. I'm still looking for it, but I'm unable to find it in the Croatian version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ah, it says, "Those new Serb members were born in Sarajevo and they are on Izetbegovic's pay list. In that way, Izetbegovic used the Presidency to promote his policy which went to the advantage of the Muslims." I claim that even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let's stop there for a moment. I appreciate we are all on the same page, literally. Is that what you said to the investigators and you said just now -- you still say that's true today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I claim that today, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me make it very clear to you, then, sir. Your claim --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me, Mr. President, I need to find a reference myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So your claim is that the Serb member of the Presidency, Mr. Kecmanovic, was paid money by Izetbegovic essentially to be influenced by Izetbegovic to go, if I can put it this way, the Muslim way? Is that what you're telling the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours. There is no surname to that effect here, and you're not going to find that surname anywhere in the statement given to the investigators of this Tribunal in 1996. And as you know, Your Honours, we have heard that there were two changes in the Serb members in the Presidency, and I think that the Prosecutor should have been much more proper in posing his question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nenad Kecmanovic was in the Presidency for barely a month. I think it might have been in July, 1992, and perhaps the beginning of August, 1992. And he left for political reasons. He left the Presidency and went to Belgrade. Therefore, Kecmanovic cannot be brought under this assertion and be included in this statement. And I stand by what I said then. I stand by that today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, I appreciate the clarification, but in fairness to you and the record, I specifically asked you the two Serbs who replaced Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic, I asked you specifically the two Serbs that replaced them, and you testified yesterday - and if I'm wrong, I'm sure the record will correct me - that Mr. Kecmanovic was one of the persons who replaced them at that time. So now, if there is a honest misunderstanding, I can accept that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you're saying it wasn't him but there are these other Serbs later that you say essentially that Mr. Izetbegovic paid under the table?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not apply to Kecmanovic. It applies to Tatjana Ljujic-Mijatovic, and she replaced Nenad Kecmanovic in an unlawful fashion. And Mirko Pejanovic too, who in a constitutional manner, together with -- came together with Kecmanovic. So Mirko Pejanovic and Tatjana Ljujic-Mijatovic. That's what my -- who my assertion and claim refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well. Let's go forward, please. In terms of the War Presidency, is it correct, sir, that during certain meetings in Geneva involving the War Presidency in July and perhaps early August, 1993, that the following persons were involved: Mr. Izetbegovic, who was a Muslim; Mr. Fikret Abdic, who was Muslim but I'll come back to in a moment; Miro Lasic, who is a Croat; Mile Akmadzic, who was a Croat; yourself, who we know you are a Croat; Mr. Pejanovic, a Serb; and Ms. Tatjana Mijatovic, a Serb? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plus Miro Lazovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was Mr. Lazovic a Serb?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Abdic, who I said I'd come back to, he wasn't any ally of Mr. Izetbegovic, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't support Alija Izetbegovic's position to any great measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So at that time, you had a Muslim on the Presidency who did not support Mr. Izetbegovic, you had three Croats, including yourself, and you had three Serbs, comprising the Presidency as of June, July, August 1993; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I want to take you to the referendum, please, for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was on -- that took place on the 29th of February and the 1st of March, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've made a point of saying that the referendum would have failed if the Croats had not supported it, voted in favour of it, the referendum for an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sir, I take it you'll agree with me the same could be true that if the Muslims had not supported it, the referendum would have also failed, would it not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the result of the referendum not having passed would have been Bosnia-Herzegovina would have remained part of the Serb-controlled Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As of February 1992, can you tell us who was part of the HDZ BiH Presidency? And to be clear, I'm talking about the political party Presidency.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the Croatian Democratic Union, at the end of December 1991, Mr. Kljuic, he resigned, and as the acting president of the president of the Croatian Democratic Union Bosnia-Herzegovina, a person was appointed at an extended meeting of the executive body of the party, and that person was Dr. Milenko Brkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say "the executive body of the party," is that the same thing as what was called the HDZ Bosnia-Herzegovina Central Board?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And how did one become a member of the Central Board?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the proposal of a narrow party body, the Executive Board -- the core of the party, actually, because there would be 30 or 40 members, and every party in the HDZ had its presidency too, the president and five vice-presidents, and those individuals were the main people in proposing cadres, both for the party peaks and within the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you: You said just now it would be this person -- to become part of the Central Board, it would be on the proposal of a narrow party body, the core of the party. So again, as of March, February 1992, who was the core body of the HDZ Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because as to the structures of the Croatian Democratic Union, I was a small municipal functionary. I wasn't -- I was neither in the Executive Board nor in the narrow core of the Presidency, so I can't remember. I was much lower down, and I can't remember who made up this core.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the language on the referendum, the referendum that was voted on for the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was not the language in the referendum that many members of the HDZ wanted, was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for a time -- actually, before the referendum took place, the Croatian Democratic Union, both in its political programme before the elections, differed somewhat with respect to the political programme of the Party of Democratic Action, the SDA, and there were some dilemmas there: whether we should join up with the political programme of the SDA party or insist upon having the referendum include part of the programme of the political party of the Croatian Democratic Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you this: Isn't it true that a vast majority of the HDZ political party wanted the referendum question, that is, if you will, the question to be put on the ballot, to be worded in a very significant way differently than the language that was actually put on the ballot? And I'll put it to you very specifically. They wanted the referendum to approve separate Croatian, Muslim, and Serbian provinces; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the usher's assistance --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give an answer to the question, because I said that I was a minor actor, politically -- in these political parties. I didn't take part on a higher level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have been cautioned not to present political views. The fact that my learned colleague, Mr. Scott, is a citizen of the United States of America, is presenting political views and waging a political discussion, not his own, but he is defending and advocating a policy which I'm not sure he fully understands himself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, he just wants to know what this witness will say about the situation at that time. I don't think Mr. Scott has any political views towards this issue. And the witness has already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with that, Your Honour, and that's why the witness was brought here. All I wanted -- I merely wanted to mention the situation I was faced with when I started asking similar questions. I've been listening to these questions very carefully, and they seem to be advocating certain political views. And this trial is largely what it is. In portion, it has been reduced to politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I must respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's very personal comment against counsel. I have not injected any political views in this case. What Mr. Krsnik has just said is completely unsupported in the record, and the Chamber can look back over the last series of questions and see that. It is absolutely without foundation, it's a personal insult, and I object to it. I also object -- I must at this time, Your Honour, pick up on the counsel's and Judge Clark's comments. I object to the repetitious objections of counsel. It's very clear that when we get into an area that Mr. Krsnik doesn't like, he interrupts the flow of the questioning. He's done it over and over again, and I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I have to tell you that some of your questions are very difficult to answer. It could be interpreted in quite a different way. So I hope you could put to this witness in a very clear and concise way your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that criticism I'll accept. I'm sure that some of my questions are not put as well as they could, and for that I apologise and will try to do better. But I object to the political characterisations made by counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I've had placed before you, I hope, Exhibit P114, which is a record of the meeting of the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina Central Board on the 9th of February, 1992. There is a B/C/S version attached to it, and I want --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could interpreters have a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Certainly. There is an extra -- Mr. Usher, are there still any extra copies that might go to the booths, to the translation booths, please? Can the translation booth assist me in whenever you're ready to proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We're ready, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to direct your attention to what I assume will be roughly the second page of the document also in the Bosnian-Serbo-Croatian language. And I'm going to direct your attention to this, and if you can find this language. It's the second item, where there's a "yes/no" under the language. Can you confirm to this Chamber, please. And there's nothing controversial about this. Please assist the Chamber. The language of the referendum that was put to a vote in February and March 1992, was that language: "Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a state of equal citizens and peoples: Croats, Muslims, Serbs, and other peoples who live in it?" Is that the language of the referendum as voted on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading here: "Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a joint state of the constitutive and sovereign Croatian, Muslim, and Serbian peoples in their ethnic areas?" And in brackets, it says "cantons," with a question mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, sir. You've gone to my second question, but not my first question. Below that on the page, if you'll scan your eyes, please, down the page on the document until you come to another paragraph that looks like that. Can you please find that one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a little blurred on my copy, blurred with ink, but it says: "Are you in favour of a sovereign and independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, a state of equal citizens and peoples: Croats, Muslims, Serbs, and other peoples, who live in it?" Is that what you mean? Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Is that the language of the referendum as voted on by the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Sir, I put it to you that it is. Do you have any reason to disagree with me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let me just clarify one point. At that time, when they were meeting on the 9th of February, 1992, I personally was in America. I was on a visit there, visiting my relatives in Los Angeles, and I returned on the eve of the elections themselves, and I cut short my stay in America precisely to be able to go out and vote in the referendum. So I cannot now say with any exactitude as to the first and second proposal. I don't remember what was on the voting slip. I just circled the "yes." I can say that. But what the actual wording was, I can't say at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Well, Witness, I'm sure if it's really disputed, we can establish what the exact phraseology was. Let me put it to you this way: Whether you were in the United States at this particular time or not, sir, you've been brought here as a very senior and knowledgeable member of the BiH Presidency and of the HDZ political party. You've indicated substantial involvement and knowledge of these areas. Based on that, I put it to you this way: It's true, isn't it, that the substantial majority -- in fact, as a result of this meeting, 140 of the persons in attendance voted in favour of the separate proposition which added the words "in their ethnic areas (cantons)." Now, that's what the HDZ party wanted in the referendum, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was so or not. What is correct is what the Croatian voters voted for, and they voted for this second proposal. Now, how many members of the HDZ there were from the Executive Board who are quoted here, listed here for this second option, the separation of the Croatian areas from the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness NA --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me take you to several paragraphs up from the end of the document, where the vote of this meeting is recorded. And there were two versions of the referendum, one that had framed by the Bosnia-Herzegovinia Assembly, the first one that I read to you. It's very clear here. There was a vote on that one, and it's reflected on the face of the document, and there was a vote on the second one, including the language "in their ethnic areas (cantons)." If you will please find that language, and I'll simply ask you a question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I object to further questioning pursuant to this document, because the witness said loud and clear that he knows nothing about it and that he wasn't even in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time when this meeting took place. So I think that any further mistreatment of the witness through this document is superfluous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no. It's not mistreatment. You have to choose your words carefully. Mr. Scott, it is true that this witness is not a first-hand witness on this very particular results of the voting. It will get us nowhere, because he said very clearly he was not present at this meeting. He was away, far away, from that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I will move on other than to say Exhibit P114 is admitted into evidence. Certainly the Chamber can read it for yourself. My only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, is it really fair to say -- on the basis of the knowledge which you have, is it really fair to say that this was the view of the HDZ party? Surely it was the view expressed by the HDZ party of Western Herzegovina and not the entire Bosnia-Herzegovina party. We have evidence of a very, very strong conflict between the Presidency and the rising force in Herzegovina at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark let me correct -- let me be very clear for the record, and I won't add any -- I'm not expressing any personal views except to say what is on the document -- what the document itself purports to be. This is a meeting of the BH - and I believe we can all agree, Bosnia-Herzegovina - HDZ central board convened in Livno on the 9th of February, 1992, and the rest of the document again speaks for itself. I certainly will not try to characterise it any more than that, except that the document then goes on to say that of those persons convened, out of 143 votes cast, 140 of them voted in favour of the proposition with the language, "In their ethnic areas (cantons)." And I understand -- I will move on past the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
