utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, shall we have the break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It's a long morning session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We will resume at 3.00 in the same courtroom. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.48 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25 Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Bring the witness, please. Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you a couple of questions about the Graz meeting. You've told us that you went -- you were a member of the delegation that attended those meetings with, among others, Radovan Karadzic and Mate Boban; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as I've asked you on similar occasions, can you just describe briefly to the Chamber how it was that you became included in these meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When leaving Sarajevo, Mate Boban -- and on the 2nd of May, 1992, I went to see him to inform him of the conversations about Cutilheiro's plan at the Butmir airport in Sarajevo on the 22nd of April, 1992, and I was interested in finding out about those political, military, and economic conditions in the HZ HB. At that point, at that time, he told me that it was very good that I had informed him about that meeting at the Butmir airport in Sarajevo, and he said that we would have to go to Graz on the 6th of May, 1992, to have a meeting with the Serbian side. And in general, he told me what would be discussed. He said that Cutilheiro's plan would be discussed, as had been concluded at the Butmir airport in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. The short answer is that you attended those meetings at the invitation or instructions of Mate Boban; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And briefly going back, I'm going to ask you a very specific question, please. When you attended this meeting at the Butmir airport in Sarajevo, you testified -- I believe you said yesterday that you went to that meeting, you headed the Croat delegation because Mr. Boban was not available. My very specific question to you, sir, is: Who asked you or appointed you to act as the head of the delegation in place of Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the delegation, of the Croatian delegation, at the talks in Butmir on the 22nd of April, 1992, it was supposed to be the president, or that is to say, the acting president of the Croatian Democratic Union. At that time that was Professor Milenko Brkic. He is the person who asked me to head the delegation in his place, because that evening, the evening before his flat had been shelled --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, all I asked you, please, was just who made you the head of that delegation, and I believe you've answered the question. Going back to the Graz meeting, the purpose of that meeting was to discuss the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina among the Serbs and the Croats; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's partially correct and it's partially incorrect. As I said -- I said what was concluded at Butmir in Sarajevo. The international --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. I'm going to cut you off. I'm going to ask the usher to please put Exhibit 126.1 in front of you, which counsel may have shown you yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But you know, sir. You were there. Isn't it true that, as a result of those meetings, basically there was an agreement, complete agreement, among the Serbs and the Croats about how Bosnia-Herzegovina should be divided except for the disagreements noted in this document? That is to say, to be very clear, what is stated here is what they did not agree to but they agreed on everything else; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that meeting, there was no agreement between the Serbian and the Croatian side, of which I was a part. No agreement about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina took place. What was discussed -- the Serbian side asked for the majority of the territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina and they asked this of the Croatian side. The Croatian side was also trying to obtain as much territory as possible when dividing Bosnia and Herzegovina, but since we had not reached an agreement about certain -- we had reached an agreement about certain elements in Bosnia-Herzegovina but there were many issues and many locations which remained a matter of contention. But there was no written record and there was no agreement that had -- that was reached on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Whether there was a written agreement or not is not my question. Let me ask with the assistance of translation, please listen to the translation of this pertinent -- parts of this document. I'm starting, for the counsel and the Chamber, top of the second page: "Our intention being to resolve peacefully and by agreement all outstanding issues including the border line between our two constituent units, the Croatian unit and the Serbian unit in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the representatives of the Croatian and the Serbian national communities have established the existence of the following specific differences as regards the working demarcation map."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. If the witness says that there was no agreement, and that there never was an agreement, then I don't understand why something is being read from the agreement, if the witness has claimed that no such agreement existed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I disagree. I think the witness is being intentionally non-responsive. He says there was no written agreement. He was there. He knows what was being discussed, and I believe I'm entitled to press him on exactly what was discussed and said at that meeting, whether it was put in writing or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that this matter is at issue. Mr. Scott, you may pursue your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness NA, I'm going to ask you a very specific question. Please listen to my question. Isn't it true, as reflected here, that among the few things that were not specifically agreed on at Graz, as stated by this report, is the exact demarcation between the Serb unit, to use the term here, and the Croat unit, in relationship to Mostar? The Serbian side considered -- wanted the division to be the Neretva River itself, while the Croatian side, the Croatian delegation, and that included you, sir, considered the entire city of Mostar to be within the Croatian unit. Now, was that discussed at the meetings in Graz or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was discussed in Graz but we always emphasised that the third side, the Muslim side -- and this discussion was held with regard to Cutilheiro's plan -- and the territorial division was a matter of contention as far as all three sides were concerned. And we said that what remained a matter of contention or what we had agreed on, we said with regard to these matters, it would be necessary to ask the third side, and in this respect, as far as the Croatian delegation is concerned, we met up with the third side in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, under either scenario, either the scenario or the position of the Serb side, which wanted the division between the Croat unit and the Serb unit to be the Neretva River itself, or, according to the Croat proposal, including the entire city of Mostar in the Croat unit, there was no position -- there was no position, there was no role whatsoever, for a Muslim unit involving the city of Mostar, under either side's proposal. True?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We suggested that with regard to Mostar, and the -- and eastern Herzegovina, not just with regard to eastern Herzegovina and Mostar but in other parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina too, where -- well, now they are saying that we were trying to agree on this, we said that it was necessary to meet with the third, that is to say the Muslim, side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: As a result -- as reflected by this document, at least, was it true -- did you leave the meeting -- did the Croatian delegation leave the meeting with a view, as stated here in paragraph number 6, "In view of the agreement outlined above, no more reasons obtain for an armed conflict between the Croatians and Serbs in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We thought, not just at that meeting -- this was our opinion, not just at this meeting but earlier on, the Croatian side also thought that there was no need to wage war for some kind of territory. We believed that it was necessary to solve this in a civilised and cultured way, to solve this problem in such a manner. And on that occasion, we said that we should -- there should no longer be military action to deal with these matters of contention, matters which were contentious for the Serbian and for the Croatian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Turning -- directing your attention -- again, just for point of reference and the Chamber's and counsel's attention, to the last page of this exhibit, did you consider it accurate that the discussions at Graz and the outcome of the meeting at Graz included a ceasefire -- looking at the second paragraph on that page -- included a ceasefire -- including a ceasefire, excuse me, will form the basis for the division of Bosnia into three separate states? Now, did you and Mate Boban and others leave Graz with the understanding that essential agreement had been reached with the exception of a few disagreements on the division of Bosnia into three separate states?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian delegation did not leave Graz, did not go to Bosnia and Herzegovina from Graz with the conviction that the Serbian side would - and they had given certain promises at this meeting - didn't leave in the belief that they would do what they said they would do. It was necessary for there to be military action between the HVO and the Serbian units, especially in Mostar and eastern Herzegovina, and around Kupres, around Bosanski Brod, which is where there was intense fighting. We thought it was necessary for these -- this fighting to stop, but nothing was done. The HVO and the Muslim units -- it was not until the 15th of June, 1992, that the HVO and the Muslim units managed to push back the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, from Mostar, and further away from Stolac, towards the Serbian areas, Trebinje, Nevesinje, and so on. So it was not until one and a half months later, and we never managed to drive them back around Bosanski Brod, but on the contrary, they took Bosanski Brod too. We weren't able to drive them away from Kupres. They took Kupres. I mentioned this yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Direct your attention to the third paragraph in that document. I'll simply ask you the same question. Isn't it true that when the Croatian delegation left these meetings, the effect of the meeting was understood to overturn the mandate of the Bosnian independence referendum for self-determination for the Bosnian state? Instead, the mandate will be reversed, Bosnia will be divided, in its place three separate states will be formed? Please, sir, just answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There was no Muslim delegation in Graz, was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could have the usher's assistance -- well, before we go to that, will you look, please -- I'm going to direct your attention - again I'll have it translated for you - but to item 2 on the second page of Exhibit 126.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apologies for perhaps causing some confusion but Mr. President if we could go back for a moment to Exhibit 126.1, there is one additional question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look at item number 2, it says this: "South of Mostar, the Croatian side considers the entire area delineated in 1939, i.e., the borders of the Hrvatska Banovina to be within the Croatian constituent unit." Will you tell the judges, please, what the Hrvatska Banovina was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hrvatska Banovina, as far as Herzegovina is concerned, covered the entire area from Metkovici through Stolac, Mostar, Jablanica, Konjic, almost the entire central Bosnia, right up to old Travnik. It excluded Zenica, and the areas of Northern Bosnia, that is to say, Bosanska Posavina, Bosanski Brod, Derventa, Modric, Samac, Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Where did the concept or the definition of the Hrvatska Banovina come from? How did that originate, the concept or territory originate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it originated in the agreement, the Macek-Cvetkovic agreement, the agreement of the former Yugoslav government of 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, is it true what's said here? Separate and apart from whether you and I agree on your answers you've given previously, was it the position of the Croat delegation that the entire area delineated in the borders of the Hrvatska Banovina was in the Croatian constituent unit? Was that your position taken at those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a position which was contrary to -- it was opposed because the Serbian side asked for the majority of the territory, which was called the Hrvatska Banovina. So we had -- there was nothing else for us to do than to refer to this distant agreement between the Serbian government, between President Cvetkovic and between Macek, the Croatian representative at that time. There was nothing else for us to do other than say that we should --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The answer to my question was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like this Trial Chamber to be explained what state was in question. 1939 was mentioned, the year 1939 was mentioned, and what sort of division was in effect in 1939. That was Yugoslavia before the war. All the circumstances should then be explained to the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott. You may clear it up for us. We got a little bit lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What boundaries did the banovina relate to, and did they come into existence, and were those in fact the boundaries of Croatia for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The banovina was called Hrvatska Banovina, and it was within Yugoslavia, what was Yugoslavia at the time, the Yugoslavia which existed from 1918 right up until 1941. And as I said, with regard to the Hrvatska Banovina, it was not until 1939 that this agreement was reached, and it lasted while all Yugoslavia was in existence. That's up until 1941.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So these boundaries for the state of Croatia were in place for approximately a two-year period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if I can have your assistance. Sorry, now that you've just sat down. With the registry's assistance, this has not been assigned a number yet. Just if you can give us whatever the next exhibit number would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Usher, if you could please put that on the ELMO, and also to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry? 89 --?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Excuse me. 899, P899.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I would like you to look at what's on the ELMO there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Your Honours. I was very patient; however, I have to raise an objection. I have to object to this manner of cross-examining the witness, because he is asking our witness, who is a factual witness, to give an expert opinion as if he were a historian, someone who specialises in history. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric, because certain questions concern historical issues does not mean we treat this witness as a historian witness. Mr. Scott, unless this issue is related to the present one, we will not accept it as evidence from the historical point of view.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's directly related, Your Honour, to the evidence of this witness. This witness has come here not as an historian but as a senior Bosnian Croat leader, and he certainly knows the history of his country, and he's indicated that, and he's explained to the Chamber already what the banovina is. And to my knowledge, from what I've understood, he's explained it properly. So he does know about it. And he's in a position now, I submit to you, to confirm that what has been placed on the ELMO, P899, shows the boundaries of Croatia, including the banovina, during 1939 and 1941.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, unless this issue is related to the present issue we were discussing about just now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour. Mr. President, if you look at Exhibit 126.1, paragraph 2, the position of the Croat delegation, which this witness just said yes, their position was that the Croatian position was that the borders should be consistent with the -- delineated in 1939, i.e., the borders of the Hrvatska Banovina to be within the Croatian constituent unit. It couldn't be more relevant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, apart from the fact that I've been hearing about the testimony from the witness on the part of the Prosecutor, I would like to know who made this map, where it was published. As far as the banovina is concerned, we will be bringing in an expert rather than listen to the testimony of our colleague, the Prosecutor. And I think that before this cross-examination, we should have received some information, and I really am interested in where this map was obtained from, what the origin of this map is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, are you challenging the authenticity of this map or do you agree with the map, I mean what's on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I could even contest its authenticity. I'm not a historian and I haven't studied maps, the divisions of the kingdom of Yugoslavia, et cetera, so I cannot now claim whether this map is authentic or not. I'm just asking for its origin. I would like to know who the author of this map is, because the borders of banovina -- this was an internal division within the Republic of Yugoslavia and later they became republics. It was a territorial division inside the kingdom of Yugoslavia. So I'm just interested in where this map comes from, who the author of this map is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I believe this map is just a kind of indicative, you know, purpose, which gives us an idea where this area is normally. Since it's related to the present issue, Mr. Scott, you may continue with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, does the map that's been placed in front of you as P899, does that show the borders of the state of Croatia during the approximate time period 1939 to 1941, including the area that was called the banovina?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in 1939, the state of Croatia did not exist, so I would like to kindly ask for the questions to be put correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I think there's some problem with your question, which is not put to this witness properly. I think first of all you have to establish the relationship between this map and what was said in that document, rather than ask the witness whether this is the boundary in 1939 to 1941. You may rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the boundary of 1939 - 1941 was called the borders of the Hrvatska Banovina, as stated in Exhibit 126.1. If this witness, who is an educated man and a senior political leader, very senior political leader, who negotiated actively with Franjo Tudjman, Mate Boban, Karadzic, other people, does not know the boundaries of this country and the boundaries that he was negotiating, actively negotiating, in 1992 and 1993, I submit respectfully to the Chamber he can tell you that. But he can tell you very quickly whether this is the correct map and the boundaries, and if it isn't, he can tell us how it's not. He's quite knowledgeable and quite able to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, but you have to rephrase your question

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm getting a lot of consultation here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was this area called, sir, the Autonomous Region Banovina of 1939?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was called the Hrvatska Banovina within the framework of the kingdom of Yugoslavia, and it was established in 1939. And that does not correspond to the present-day borders of the Republic of Croatia, because there are territories there shown on this map as being part of Hrvatska Banovina. There's no Istria, for instance, which is today part of the Republic of Croatia. There's no Zadar. There are some islands missing which in those days belonged to Italy, so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to cut you off. I'm going to cut you off. You know exactly what I'm asking you. In terms of what is the Herzegovinian region - not talking about other parts of what may or may not be present-day Croatia - in talking about Herzegovina and what you know exactly this map to be -- and I put it to you, sir, you know exactly what I'm asking, you're not assisting this Chamber, and you're doing it intentionally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can I put the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You certainly may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Boras, would you look at that map in front of you. Does that represent to be what you understood to be the banovina between 1939 and 1941?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, as far as Herzegovina is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Clark. I think I put that exact question to him about ten minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Isn't it the case, sir, that those boundaries, as reflected on this map, bear a very, very close resemblance to the borders claimed by the Croatian Republic and the Croatian Community and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna as reflected on P3.4, which the Chamber saw this morning? And if need be, we can put them side by side. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true, with the addition that in this area here that we are talking about, the Croatian Community, or rather, the Croatian Democratic Union, and the 1990 elections in the month of November, they won power in these areas, and that is why the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which later became the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, in negotiations with representatives of the international community, included these areas which we are now talking about as being areas which should belong to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. The declaration of the existence of the Croatian Herceg-Bosna on the 18th of November, 1991 had nothing to do with the plans or approval of the international community, did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The international community, starting from the Cutilheiro plan --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and on through all the other plans --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're not --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like you to instruct the witness to give responsive answers. This has gone on long enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, first of all, we have to let the witness continue. If, after a few sentences, he is out of the track, we'll advise him to be direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can tell you what he's already said has nothing to do with the Cutilheiro plan. It has absolutely nothing to do. And that's how he started out his answer. I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. The problem is that maybe you, the witness, and Defence counsel, know all the background, all the issues, but the Judges don't know at all. We have to hear a little bit of his answering, and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. later on we'll make the judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, of course I appreciate that, but again, let me just repeat the question I did ask him specifically, and if he answers specifically that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the declaration of the existence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna on the 18th of November, 1991 had nothing to do with the plans or approval of the international community, did it? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither yes or no, without a certain explanation. With your permission, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm in the Court's hands, but I don't want to spend -- waste any more of my examination time in arguing with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let the witness continue. Yes, you may give us a very short, concise explanation of your answer, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was officially formed on the 18th of November, 1991, and that is while Yugoslavia was still in existence, as was Bosnia-Herzegovina as part of Yugoslavia. And when the area of that Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was attacked by the Yugoslav People's Army and by other Serb paramilitary units, an organisation was formed for those regions that we now have called the Croatian Banovina, to liberate them or to defend them from the Serb aggression. However, later on, the international plans starting from the Cutilheiro plan onwards took that into consideration in all their versions. This applied to Cutilheiro, Vance-Owen, Owen-Stoltenberg and even later the Washington Agreements. So that is my explanation, and that is the truth as I see it, which I have come to convey here to Your Honours, rather than answering questions of this kind that I simply am unable to answer in the way that the Prosecution would like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, were there representatives of the international community attending the meetings on the 18th of November, 1991, when the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was declared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not, nor could they have, because Yugoslavia was still in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've been very critical of Mr. Izetbegovic for supposedly acting in a dual capacity. You said yesterday whether he was acting as the member of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina or if he was acting as a representative of the SDA. Didn't you do exactly the same thing a number of times, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, when you were in Graz, were you representing the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina or were you representing the Bosnian Croats and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was representing the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You testified yesterday - and indicated again a few moments ago - that the Croat side was adamant in its position at Graz, and I take it when you say you were adamant, that you were adamant about the boundaries being of the banovina. Why were you so adamant about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were adamant because the Serb side asked for the impossible. Within Bosnia-Herzegovina, through the Serb autonomous regions, four of such regions had already subjugated and placed under their control more than 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was not enough for them, so they even wanted what the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna had defended, that is the areas around Mostar, areas in Bosanska Posavina, that is Bosanski Brod, Derventa, and these were still under the control of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Samac, Orasje and Brcko. So they wanted that too. 70 per cent was not sufficient for them. They wanted up to 90 per cent in Graz, if we had let them have it as the Croatian community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you would let them have it. Why didn't you compromise with the Serbs? Wouldn't that have been in the interests of peace?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we had wanted to do that, we wouldn't have had a referendum. We wouldn't have taken part in the referendum in February and the beginning of March in 1992. And then the Serb side would have had the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the framework of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, my question to you is: Weren't the Muslims entitled to be just as adamant about their position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what was it exactly - can you just tell the Chamber - was the source of the disagreement or the nature of the disagreement about between Mate Boban and Dario Kordic and people like Ivan Bender and Stjepan Kljujic and his part of the party? What were their different visions of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me say first of all, Stjepan Kljujic, being a citizen of Sarajevo, supported Alija Izetbegovic in every respect, and his political option was an unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What do you mean -- sorry, I'm going to cut you off and take this in smaller pieces. When you say "unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina" -- as the Chamber said, assist them in understanding this more, please. When you say "unitary," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: A unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina means a strictly centralised state without regionalisation, without respect of the specifics of various areas within Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it would be centralised power and authority without counties, cantons, regions, but simply a Bosnia-Herzegovina and municipalities within it. This suited the political options of the Muslim people, or rather Alija Izetbegovic, who represented the Muslim people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... nothing about the Muslims. My question to you was the differences between Mate Boban and his group, if you will, on the one hand, and Mr. Kljujic and his member -- and his followers, if you will, if I can use that terminology, among the Bosnian Croats, for the vision of what Bosnia-Herzegovina should be. If I can assist you further, isn't the basic difference, Mr. Kljujic was for, as you say, a unit -- a single, unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina, and what Mate Boban and Dario Kordic and you and Ivan Bender wanted was a Bosnia-Herzegovina divided up into three separate ethnic states?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have just answered, Mr. Prosecutor, what the political options of Stjepan Kljujic were, and you asked me about Stjepan Kljujic. And I just told you the positions advocated by Stjepan Kljujic. And now I can tell you what were the positions advocated by Boban, Kordic and Bender, the persons you named, if I may, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please do, briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the programme of the party of the Croatian Democratic Union, at first, there were provisions for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina within the framework of Yugoslavia as a confederal state, and such a confederal state of Bosnia-Herzegovina should have been a decentralised one consisting of three federal units, because we had three constituent peoples. In a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina, equality of all three constituent peoples could not be achieved, and especially of the Croatian people, who were less numerous. They accounted for only 17.5 per cent of the total population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the event of an unitary system of government, the Croatian people would very quickly disappear from those parts. They would be outnumbered by the Muslim people, who already, in 1991, accounted for 44 per cent of the population, and already in their political platform regarding the internal structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Croatian people could not allow -- and even to this day, there is dispute over this, by the Croatian people and with reference to the Dayton agreement, a just solution has been found for any one of the three peoples and especially not for the Croatian people. Even now, five or six years after Dayton, the same questions and the same problems are being addressed and raised today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't interrupt you one time in that last answer, so I want to go back and put my earlier question to you. I suggest with the explanation you've already given, you can answer this yes or no. The vision of Mate Boban and others with him were for a Bosnia-Herzegovina divided up into three sovereign ethnic states and the vision held by Mr. Kljujic and others with him was for a single, unified, multi-ethnic Bosnia-Herzegovina. That's the basic difference, isn't it? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Three sovereign --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You've answered my question. I'm sure counsel will ask you -- give you an opportunity to explain it further. If you say no, the Judges will decide based on all the evidence. Sir, isn't it the fact that anyone who opposed - and I submit to you you did this just a few moments ago yourself in reference to Mr. Kljujic - anyone who wasn't part of the Boban-Kordic-Bender-Boras view of Bosnia-Herzegovina was labelled as pro-Izetbegovic and pro-Muslim, and people like Mr. Klujic, people like Milivoje Gagro, people like Dragutin Cicak were forced out of the party because they didn't fit into the divided Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were pacifists who did not, from the beginning, defend Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. Among those pacifists, there were some Croats too, but fewer in number, headed by Stjepan Klujic. The majority of the political representatives of the Croatian people in 1991, 1992 and so on, were activists, who, from the very first day, opposed the Serb aggression on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, especially against Croatian areas which were not protected by the Presidency as a whole, but on their own initiative, organised resistance in enterprises, and thank God they managed to preserve about 30 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not to be conquered by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself. It's pacifists not -- passive people, not those in favour of peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, it was -- among other things, it was Franjo Tudjman who backed Mate Boban after -- instead of Mr. Kljujic and saw that Mr. Kljujic was removed from the party; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you can assist the Chamber with this, sir. When was it that the Bosnian Muslims that lived in the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna, when did they get to vote for Herceg-Bosna? They didn't, did they, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one had an occasion. There was no voting for Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the form of any kind of elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Exactly. And when did the Bosnian Muslims that lived within the territory claimed by Herceg-Bosna, when were they given the opportunity to vote for Mate Boban?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never had this opportunity. Nor did I as a Croat have an opportunity to vote for Mate Boban.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mate Boban was put in power purely and simply by Franjo Tudjman, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, can we put Exhibit P175 in front of the witness, please? I believe that one will have -- we'll need the -- please, thank you. Mr. Usher, if you can give one to the witness, that is if there is a Bosnian-Serbo-Croatian version and if another version can be perhaps put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you attended a meeting of the central Bosnia HVO on the 22nd of September, 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And Exhibit 175, which are the excerpts from the minutes of that meeting, on the first page, on the list of attendees, you were listed about three-fourths of the way down through that list, Franjo Boras, member of the B and H Presidency. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this meeting was chaired -- or the working presidents of this meeting included Dario Kordic, Anto Valenta, Tihomir Blaskic and Ignac Kostroman, and were they four of the -- or perhaps the four principal HVO leaders in central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Chamber that what we have here -- and you can look at it if you like, please. I put it to you that this is a virtual progress report on the status of the HVO takeover of each municipality in central Bosnia. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer with a yes or no without a brief introduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well let me direct your attention to the second page, the section of the report called "Novi Travnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: With the usher's assistance, that's on the second page. Perhaps the -- if you can lower it down a bit on the ELMO and perhaps the booth can zero in on that paragraph, the Novi Travnik section, that anyone who doesn't have a hard copy in front of them -- can we zero in tighter on the section, Novi Travnik? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The report on Novi Travnik, for instance, was, "It is estimated that the HVO holds about 70 per cent authority while the Muslims hold about 30 per cent." Can you go down to Vitez, please? Simply going to take you to certain parts of the document and then I'll ask you questions about it. Wasn't it being reported to the Bosnian Croat central Bosnia HVO that, "In Vitez there is still dual authority. There is a possibility of confrontation between the Croats and the Muslims because of the HVO's taking power"? If I can direct your attention to the third page, to the section of the report coming from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, my apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To the section on Fojnica, going down to the third sentence or so? "Schools have not started operating in the Croatian language." Several lines down below that, "Roads being built. It will not go through any Muslim villages." Report for Bugojno on the next page, Bugojno, please? Next to last line or so, "The Croatian dinar is an accepted means of payment, just as in all the municipalities of central Bosnia from Travnik to Kresovo." Busovaca. That was the home municipality of Dario Kordic, wasn't it? "HVO authority was set up on the 9th of May, 1992. HVO is the only authority." I will only pick one other particular example for now. On Kiseljak, on the next page, the very last sentence in the report on Kiseljak: "Elementary and secondary schools have started working in the Croatian language." Now, we could spend a lot of additional time on this document, but, sir, I put it to you what this document is about is report on the status and the progress of the HVO takeover of the municipalities in central Bosnia in a very detailed respect, and you were there and attended this meeting, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially correct. And, yesterday in answer to questions from the attorney, I commented on this document. I just happened to be at this meeting by chance on my way back from Kakanj - and Kakanj is a predominantly Muslim town with a coal mine and a thermal power station. In the morning, at the invitation of the director of the mine, I went there, and they asked me -- the miners asked me to bring some influence to bear on their municipal leadership. So that the thermal power station could start working so that the power produced could be sent to Croatia, the southern parts of Croatia, or rather, Dalmacija, where, in those days, there were more than 200.000 Muslim refugees. And Croatia was short of electricity at that time, because it was surrounded on all sides. Please allow me --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to cut you off. This has nothing to do with my question. You were at this meeting. It's actually reflected on the next-to-the-last page. We can find that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object. The witness has, on several occasions, said that he was there by chance and that after a brief period he left the meeting, and now he's being forced to give answers that would suit the Prosecutor. The witness has said this three times. He wanted to say that once again now, and he was not allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, ask this witness what does he mean by "chance to be present at that meeting," and how long he stayed during that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Witness, you've heard the President's questions. You've already told us you happened to be in the area, and how long did you stay at the meeting, are you going to tell us now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the meeting for about half an hour. Dario Kordic asked me to inform them about what I had done and tell them whether I had managed to successfully carry out the work in Kakanj, which had to do with supplying electricity to the southern parts of Croatia, parts in which there were over a thousand refugees of Muslim nationality and from Eastern Bosnia, Northern Bosnia. Of course, they put me down in the record. They entered me in the record immediately, as I was present at that meeting, and I informed them about that. And I had to carry on towards Mostar for this meeting at 1400 hours. And I left this meeting. I don't know what was discussed there. This is something that I'm not at all familiar with, because after half an hour I told them what I had spoken about in Kakanj. I said goodbye to them. And I had hundreds of meetings like this with representatives of the Croatian people and representatives of the Muslim people, and hundreds of meetings, joint meetings, of theirs, where common problems were discussed in this area of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you one further question about this document before we have to move on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the last page in the English version, Mr. Usher, second paragraph on the last page. It says "refugee camps are not acceptable."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can, sir, can you assist the Chamber in understanding why it was that refugee camps were not acceptable in the areas controlled by the Central Bosnia HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about these refugee camps. I don't know where they were. I don't know when they were established. I don't know anything about these camps, these refugee camps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've testified in the course of the last several days that Mr. Izetbegovic released you or discharged you from your position in the Presidency in about October 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reality, sir, you had, for all practical purposes, withdrawn from the Presidency in early August 1993, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, let me, with the usher's assistance, hand you what's been marked as Exhibit 555.3. I have copies that can be distributed as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Almost using your time, how long do you expect for your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look behind it, sir, you'll see that there's the B/C/S version. Mr. President, I would hope that, with the difficulties that we've encountered here, that I've encountered here, at least, I think it will take another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you really want us to sit until 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I would like to do it as short as possible, but that's been more a question of the witness's answers than my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Try to put concise questions to this witness. You may continue, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've now been handed Exhibit P555.3. This is a copy of a letter that you and Mr. Lasic and Mr. Akmadzic signed -- or a statement to the press. Let me -- forgive me, not letter. Statement to the press the three of you made on the 3rd of August, 1993, announcing that you were not going to participate, is the word here in the second paragraph, have decided not to participate in the work of the Presidency until the offensive of the Muslim army, et cetera. And you see that there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in the Croatian version it doesn't say that this was sent to the media, and words are again being put into his mouth, or rather, questions are being asked, and this is why I am objecting. Why does the Prosecutor think that this was sent to the media? That's the first question. This document should first be identified. It should be verified. One shouldn't claim from the very start something that is not stated anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I answer this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with this statement, the members of the War Presidency who were representing the Croatian people, we wanted to say that we would not participate in the work of the Presidency until the offensive launched by the Muslim army ceased, that is to say, the BH army, the offensive of the BH army against the Croatian population in Central Bosnia, because the Presidency was the Supreme Commander of that army. So we were suspending -- the members of the Croatian people in the Presidency, we were suspending our work in the Presidency while the fighting between the army and the HVO was ongoing. So we did not resign. We were only suspending our work for our membership of the Presidency for a certain period of time, and this Presidency was the Supreme Command, in fact, of the BH army. We simply did not want to participate in it, but in no way did we resign, and as soon as these hostilities ceased, we would return to the Presidency. But circumstances were such that the hostility soon came to an end, the hostilities between the army and the HVO. There was the Washington Agreement, and fortunately for both peoples that conflict came to an end, and the suspension of our membership in the Presidency too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, the document is titled "Statement to the Press --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your mike, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The document itself is titled "Statement to the Press," and it is in fact your signature -- on the original B/C/S version, does it have your signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. That is not stated in the Croatian language. What the Prosecutor has just said is not in the Croatian version. The translation that we have -- or rather, the original is probably Croatian. It doesn't state that it is a statement for the press.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what are the last three sentences in the Croatian version, and the name and the signature?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 3rd of August, 1993, and not at the request of the President of the HZ HB, Mate Boban. At the negotiations in Geneva, we shall be as part of the Croatian negotiating team. Geneva, the 2nd of August, 1993. Signatures. For the information of the co-chairmen of the international conference, Lord David Owen and Mr. Thorwald Stoltenberg. That is all that is stated in the Croatian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that a problem of translation, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the English version, that's not written down in the English version. It doesn't state that it's in Geneva, and the signatures aren't there, and it also doesn't say that it was provided to Lord David Owen and to Mr. Stoltenberg for their information. That simply is not contained in the English version, and it has not been translated into the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, is there an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The explanation is this is the document as was received by us. It's not a question of translation. This was the document that we contend was distributed. And I'll ask some questions to the witness. I suspect it may not be helpful, but I'll ask anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you were in Geneva and there were press statements being made at that time, was it common for press statements to be prepared by you and other delegations in the English language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. As I said, sir, it is your signature on the B/C/S version; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the B/C/S text, what it says there, and the part that the President asked you to read a moment ago, that is the statement that the three of you signed on the 2nd of August, 1993; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you're telling us that -- and you've already told the President on that day, or beginning the following day, you left the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina delegation and joined the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban, and joined his delegation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, you say that you were protesting the fighting of the ABiH against the HVO. Did you consider, sir -- did you ever make such a protest or suspend your membership in the Presidency when the HVO was attacking the Muslim communities in the Lasva Valley and in Herzegovina in April, May 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of the fact that the HVO attacked Muslim areas in Central Bosnia, and the last time I came was on the 26th and the 27th of March, 1993. That was the last time I went to Zenica, for talks with the representative of the 3rd Corps, Mr. Hadzihasanovic. I went there together with Tihomir Blaskic, at the request of Ejub Ganic, and he was supposed to be at that meeting too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm in the Chamber's hands at this point. If the Chamber simply wants the witness to continue on giving long answers, I will not make any effort to intervene. And really, it is in the Chamber's hands. I asked a very simple question, and now we're talking about that he went to a meeting sometime in March on something else. If the Chamber wants to hear it, of course the Chamber can hear whatever it wants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think it's clear that this witness, in response to what you asked him, denies any activity by the HVO against the Muslim population. We'll take on board what his answer is. If he wants to elaborate on that, I think it's his style, and he is a man of a certain age. We'll give him, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just ask about a couple of specific things to see if it might prompt your memory, sir. After the HVO killed over a hundred civilians in the village of Ahmici on the 16th of April, 1993, did you consider suspending your membership in the Presidency as a protest against that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was not aware of what had happened in that area, and so I was not aware of what happened in Ahmici either.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to stop you there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither did I think about --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're telling this Chamber that the massacre in Ahmici, which was reported literally around the world the day after it happened, and brought tremendous pressure to bear on President Tudjman and the state of Croatia, you didn't hear about that? You didn't know about what happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about what had happened in Ahmici, but I didn't know who had committed that act, those acts. I lived in Mostar. All ties had been -- all lines of communication had been cut off. And I still don't know whether it has been determined who was responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, on the 9th of August, 1993, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna passed a decision to the effect that the Croat members of the Presidency would no longer participate in the Presidency. So in fact, this wasn't simply your individual act, was it? This was a political statement and act taken by the Croatian Republic - or excuse me - at this time still the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And you were instructed, in so many words, to withdraw, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of such a decision, and I was never informed of such a decision. I personally considered myself to be a member of the Presidency right up until October. It was about the 20th of October, 1993, right up until that date, when I was dismissed by Alija Izetbegovic. And I found out about that decision perhaps three or four months later, when I saw on the television -- I saw that some members of the War Presidency appeared on television and they hadn't been candidates for the War Presidency. I even saw Kljuic, Stjepan Kljuic, who had resigned, and then entered the War Presidency once again. So therefore, I can freely say that they were making -- they were turning the War Presidency into some kind of a circus.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, do you really want this Chamber to believe that you were surprised to be dismissed from the Presidency in October 1993, after you had left the Presidency delegation, you had joined the Bosnian Croat delegation, you had aligned yourself with Mate Boban, who was the president of a self-proclaimed Herceg-Bosna, the armed forces of which were fighting against and killing government soldiers? Is it so surprising that the head of that government would dismiss you from the Presidency in those circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think this is a question. I think the Prosecutor is giving testimony. And in any case, I think that by simplifying the situation in the former Yugoslavia and in Bosnia and Herzegovina, by simplifying it in the way that the Prosecutor is doing, I think that he's attempting to obtain simplified answers. And if this were common practice, we would have solved the problems a long time ago and this Tribunal wouldn't be in existence. So this is why I'm raising an objection and, in particular, why I'm objecting to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, would you please skip this question. We could arrive at the conclusion by ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just wanted to request a break, out of respect for the witness's age, if possible. That's the only reason. Because I can see that he is getting tired now and that it is a bit difficult for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we'll resume at a quarter to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Bring in the witness, please. Mr. Krsnik, I know you are tired. How long do you think your re-examination will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everyone's asking me that today, but I think that perhaps I won't have any at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what will happen during this last hour and how long this will go on for, but if it continues as it has been, I don't think I will have any re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, during the time that you were in Mostar - and I allow that you were away on business on a number of occasions - but nonetheless, from approximately May, 1992 forward, until the end of 1993, in the time you were there, you were aware, were you not, that there was sustained shelling and fighting going on in the city of Mostar and that in particular, there was the Muslim enclave in -- called East Mostar; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you told us one occasion in your testimony earlier about some soldiers coming to your building to evict some people who lived there. Did you see other things like that happening, not necessarily in your building, but wasn't that a common occurrence during the second half of 1993 at least? Weren't Muslim families in fact being evicted all over Mostar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I saw in my building, I have told you about. As for other examples, I didn't see any because I frequently went outside Mostar performing my duties as a member of the Presidency. And it was dangerous to move around, especially at night, and even during the daytime, around Mostar. So that I cannot say that there were similar incidents such as the one I saw in my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, tell the Chamber, please, approximately how many days - and I realise it's sometime ago; I'm only asking for an approximation - from approximately let's say the 1st of May, 1993, until the end of the year of 1993, how many days were you away from Mostar? Ten? Fifteen? Thirty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we were to add it all up, it would be about half a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you're telling this Chamber that throughout all that period, the only time you saw anything happening of the type that I've described to you is the one incident where you've described when the soldiers came into your building? Other than that, you didn't see anything else happening in Mostar throughout this period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stand by what I said, only in my building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever know someone named Dunja Bosnjic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosnjic, Dunja yes, I do know him. He's from my building. He's a neighbour. Or rather her husband, Mr. Safet Bosnjic. He was a colleague of mine in my enterprise, and also he's a neighbour. He lives in the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that true? Does he live in that same building today, he and his wife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He lives in Eastern Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Safet Bosnjic, in fact, was one of the men who were arrested and taken and held at the Heliodrom, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And he was being held there at the end of August, 1993, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly until when, but he was given an opportunity to return to West Mostar, where he lived, to my building that I lived in, or to go to East Mostar, and he chose to go to East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When was he given this choice, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose while he was at the Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On what conditions are you suggesting that he could be released? Could he just simply walk out of the Heliodrom whenever he wanted to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, you were present in the building when his wife, Dunja Bosnjic, was evicted from her flat, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I wasn't present. The day before that I was in Zagreb. And the next day, in the morning, I returned from Zagreb, and my wife and son informed me that some people had come to pick up Mr. Safet's wife and a son, I think, and that they had been taken and moved to Eastern Mostar. I was sorry about that. If I had been there that night, I believe I would have prevented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, what's your understanding, if you have any at all, as to why Mrs. Bosnjic was evicted and taken from her apartment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume to meet up with her husband on the eastern side, because later she would come to see me in my apartment several times, and she even asked me to go with her to her former apartment. However, a person I didn't know had moved into that apartment who was of a rather doubtful character. So with Dunja, we used to be friends, house friends. We used to visit one another. So I couldn't assist her in that respect, but she did drop in several times to my home and we had coffee, together with my wife. But Safet never crossed to Western Mostar, nor did he come and visit me in my apartment, as his wife, Dunja, did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And is it true that once they were -- when she was evicted from the flat, they never lived there again after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They haven't returned to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And the man who moved into the flat that morning was an HVO soldier, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to ask --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find him or meet him as a soldier, and I never saw him later wearing a soldier's uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll ask the usher's assistance, please, to distribute Exhibit 578.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I've had placed before you an SIS information - that's what it's titled - dated the 26th of August, 1993, and you'll see in the second page that there is a B/C/S version?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And just for the Chamber's and counsel's benefit, you'll see that -- this is a situation I wanted to indicate to the Chamber. We have two very, very similar documents, as the Court has seen before. The text is the same. The first one has letterhead and other markings, and you'll note in the upper right-hand corner the archive stamp. The second original B/C/S document, the same text, also an archive stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we see this document for the first time. We always ask to be treated equally as the Prosecutor, so at least we could have been given this before the beginning of the cross-examination. And again, this is some sort of intelligence information from archives in Zagreb. And especially as this is a document of that kind, we should have been given it before the cross-examination. Surely the Defence could have been given time to familiarise itself. There's no stamp or signature again, just a document written by some intelligence service, in this case, by the SIS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is this the first time to furnish us with this document, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. This is cross-examination. The Defence has not provided us with a single document. Maybe the Chamber -- Your Honours, I won't do it now, suggest we do it now, of course, before the witness, but it may be helpful for us to discuss the matter of the documents, Your Honour. Because frankly, this is cross-examination. We have been provided no disclosure whatsoever, and yet I'm being told constantly that we have to turn over everything before the cross-examination starts. Now, those are brand new rules to me, both in this Tribunal and elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's interesting to hear the Prosecutor interpreting things as they suit him. I obey the rulings of this Chamber, as well as the Statute and the rules of behaviour. We have been given the ruling of this Chamber that we have to turn over to you all documents before the cross-examination, and we have done that. Let me remind you of things that were not translated, for instance the videotape. All the documents that we used we had to turn over to you prior to the cross-examination, and what has that to do with the disclosure? And before the Prosecution said we are not obliged to disclose because we haven't reached any such agreement with the Defence. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, as I said, I don't want to take -- especially at this hour, take the necessary time to discuss the matter. I suggest it might be something for further discussion. But this document -- the witness can very clearly indicate -- he's already told us, in fact - and the document speaks for itself and has essentially already been authenticated -- he's described the events, he's described the witness's name. It is, in fact, the correct address which he's testified to. There is no reason to question the authenticity of this document. And counsel -- it's again one of these incidents simply where counsel doesn't like the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, please, I like what I see, in fact. Because an unknown spy, is - look at his initials - is saying that the witness is a reliable source of his information. So somebody reporting under these initials to a SIS centre in Mostar is just saying that the witness is a reliable source, and we see this for the first time. I like this very much, in fact, because it shows how things are being done. Only you should have given it to us prior to your cross-examination. You see what it says on this document very clearly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, we are not going to debate on this issue. I think earlier on this Trial Chamber has made a ruling, I'll reiterate our rulings in your case, that if you want to use a document in the cross-examination, you have to show it to the other party and to the Chamber beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I can only note for the record that was never done by the Defence during cross-examination. We didn't receive a single -- we never received a single exhibit before the cross-examination started. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is not true, and I protest emphatically. I cannot say how -- see how things can be uttered in this courtroom. I will now ask all transcripts to be verified. This is impermissible. I'm sorry, maybe you were consulting. What my learned friend has just now said is not true, and I protest that the truth can be evaded in this way. At least we have a transcript. How can this be allowed in this courtroom, to evade the truth in this way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, what I'm saying was that if you want to use a document before -- in the cross-examination, you have to show us before that. You have to inform us what kind of documents you are going to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And especially concerning with those documents which the authenticity is in question. So my advice is that you withdraw this document and change the subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you said a moment ago that you could -- there was nothing you could do to help this woman. Surely a person as powerful as you could have gone to the authorities, you could have gone to Mr. Boban, like you told us you did the first time, and done something to help this Muslim family, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm so sorry, we are all tired. These are speculations and the witness is being asked to speculate, and that is my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, it's not a speculation. It's a very natural question that the Prosecution asked. We want to know the answer, but actually, I believe that this witness has partially answered this question, but let us hear what this witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have nothing more to say than what I've already said, and that is that Mr. Safet Bosnjic -- let me not repeat the fact that he was a friend of mine, that at the Heliodrom, he decided not to return to Western Mostar but went to Eastern Mostar, that his wife and one, I think, child, one night, as I was coming back from Zagreb, that night, she was evicted to the eastern side, that only upon returning from Zagreb that morning, I learnt from my wife and my son that Mrs. Bosnjic had gone to the eastern side. I know nothing more. If I had been there that night in the building, I would have tried to do everything in my power, even risking my own life, as I had done before under much more difficult circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you complain to any authority, any Bosnian Croat authority, about the treatment given to this family? Did you go to any -- did you go to the police station? Did you go to Mr. Boban? Did you go to the head of the HVO? Did you go to anyone -- sorry, sir, I wasn't finished my question. Did you go to anyone seeking some assistance for this family that you say you were so anxious to give?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as I had a chance, and two or three days later, I happened to have met with Mr. Boban in Grude on some other business, and I informed him about Mr. Bosnjic and his wife, and he said to me, "Find out. If they wished to return to Western Mostar, to their apartment, I will, through certain channels, arrange it." And on the basis of this promise, I sent a message to Mrs. Bosnjic and Mr. Safet, if they wished to return, I would guarantee that they could come back to the apartment in which they used to live. However, they did not come back to this day. Nor are they insisting on the flat being returned to them. In Eastern Mostar, they were given quite a decent apartment, and as far as I know, if they insisted on this flat being restored to them for them to come back and live in it, then I think they could have achieved that long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you go with information to the SIS on a number of occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No information with SIS. Nor do I know what SIS was, nor where it was, nor did I ever discuss anything at all with people from SIS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You don't know what SIS was is what you're telling this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you're asking me. I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you've already told us that you attended a meeting in Zagreb on the 8th of January, 1992, with President Tudjman and others; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in fact you arranged that meeting on rather short notice, you told us, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So you have the ability to make a personal telephone call to the President of the Republic of Croatia and arrange a meeting on very short notice; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you've told us about this meeting was to discuss certain discussions that you'd previously had with this Serbian man named Koljevic about the division of Bosnia Herzegovina into different ethnic states; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you knew, by the way, that this meeting was being recorded? Everyone in the meeting knew it was being recorded, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
