utterances.text: And in fact, one of Mr. Tudjman's aides, Mr. Manolic asked Mr. Koljevic, didn't he, "Is it okay with you if we tape-record this?" And Mr. Koljevic said, "Sure, no problem"; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I ask the witness to be provided, please, Exhibit PT3, the -- specifically for the witness's sake, of course, the B/C/S version is the presidential transcript dated the 8th of January, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Direct your attention, sir, in the first couple of pages of the Bosnian-Serbo-Croatian version, the conversation involving Mr. Manolic, Mr. Koljevic, primarily the two of them initially, and it's correct - just Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to confirm what we talked about in the last few minutes - that the discussion of the tape recording of the conversation was specifically discussed and approved by Mr. Koljevic, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I repeat to you again, sir, the purpose of this meeting or what was discussed at this meeting was Mr. Koljevic's proposals and other proposals that had previously been discussed about the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina into three ethnic states; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not earlier on, but at this very meeting, without any preparation on paper, Mr. Koljevic came out with this idea, and he came to Zagreb, and for the first time at this meeting he conveyed this idea of his on the internal structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And he presented it as an idea, but in a confusing sort of manner. He was a highly intelligent writer, but legally, in legal terms, he was unable to express what he actually meant and how he envisaged those three states. But in any event, in this idea of his, Bosnia-Herzegovina was retained, as well as the central institutions of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in an extremely decentralised manner. And he proposed three states within Bosnia-Herzegovina: a Muslim state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a Croatian state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a Serbian state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But he didn't really explain what territory the Croatian state would consist of, the Serbian state, or the Muslim state, but only in the legal sense he presented this idea. And then the hosts started putting questions: How could this be carried out, what are the problems involved, and so on. Koljevic himself said, if you read the whole transcript, which again does not really reflect everything, or maybe it was not transcribed properly -- but as I have already said, he presented it in a confusing manner, and one cannot say how this would be implemented. I can't find the exact place where he himself said, "I don't know how this would be realised." Then the hosts say, "As this has not been prepared properly, we should leave it to experts to analyse the idea in detail and to put it on paper, and then, as such, we could discuss it." Then Koljevic goes on to say that for this idea to be put into effect, the municipality structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina needed to be reorganised, because it was done during the Communist era, at the expense of both the Croatian and the Serb peoples. So this idea of his about three states within Bosnia-Herzegovina, I say again, would entail the prior reconstruction of the unfair structure of municipalities, which, he said, were at the expense of the Serb and the Croatian people. Then I mentioned Mostar and Dobratici, near Stari Travnik. Dobratici, with a population of some 5.000 inhabitants, was separated from Stari Travnik, which it used to belong to, and was attached to Kulen-Vakuf, where there was a Muslim majority. And Dobratici -- the Croatian population then becomes a minority in Kulen-Vakuf, and Stari Travnik is then transformed into a municipality with a Muslim majority. So the Croatian people in Travnik, instead of being a majority, becomes a minority. So this was a tendentious Communist idea for Bosnia and Herzegovina, through the composition of the municipalities, to be made, as much as possible, a Muslim republic. We had a similar situation in Mostar. A village of Dolac was separated from Mostar and attached to Siroki Brijeg, whereas Jablanica, which already had a Muslim majority, Dreznica was separated from it and attached to Mostar. So that in an artificial manner, the municipality of Mostar had a Muslim majority. Before these events, the Croats were in the majority in Mostar. There was a similar situation in Banja Luka, as Koljevic said, mentioning some examples. So this idea was valid in Zagreb only, and upon returning from Zagreb, nothing more was done about it. I informed Mr. Kljuic about these discussions when I returned, and I think he still hadn't handed over his duties to Dr. Milenko Brkic. And I also informed Alija Izetbegovic what we had discussed. And two days later, Koljevic came to my office and said nothing will come of that idea. Mr. Milosevic does not agree with this idea that he had presented in Zagreb. And that is all it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You're not suggesting to this Chamber, sir, that all this was put on the table by Mr. Koljevic for the very first time, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the very first time when he came up with an idea like this. However, in the course of 1991, he, as a member of the Presidency, was preoccupied with Bosnia and Herzegovina and with transforming it into a state similar to Switzerland. He thought differently than Karadzic, Krajisnik especially, or Milosevic, because he truly wanted to preserve Bosnia-Herzegovina as such but only to decentralise it as much as possible and to make it more decentralised, preserving the traditions, culture, economic and traffic and so on, not exclusively on ethnic principles. However, with this idea, he went a step further than cantonisation, which is why he was unable to explain it. When Mr. Lerotic [phoen] asked him, for example, "How can this be carried out, Mr. Koljevic? How can be it implemented?" he replied, "I don't know myself." As far as I can remember, there is a place where he says, "I don't know myself." And then it was said, "Well, this idea has not been worked out in detail. When you go back to Sarajevo, set up a group of experts to develop the idea, and when it's developed, then we'll see whether we can discuss it or not. However, Cutilheiro's plan followed, other ideas arrived, and this idea was laid aside and was not discussed any further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that these concepts had been discussed many times before, including at Karadjordjevo, between the Serbs and the Croats, they were discussed many times thereafter, and in fact, in a nutshell, this was indeed both the Croat and the Bosnian Croat plan for the division of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I said - and I am glad it was repeated on two occasions by my learned friend - I brought this witness here to testify to events within his own experience, and I did not depart from that. The witness is now asked to speculate about Karadjordjevo. The witness cannot know this. Now he's asked to present his opinions and to speculate. That is why I object to this form of questioning, which we have been listening to for a few hours now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, the witness said that for the very first time, as a member of the Presidency, he put forward this plan. No matter if you agree with it or not, we will take it as what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, I understand that, Your Honour. I do understand that we are to put our case to the witness, and I simply meant to indicate to this witness that our case is contrary to what he has said. We put it to him that the version he has given us is not supported by the facts at all. But that's all. It was simply to put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in terms of -- if we can go forward --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please, when they say "our case," when has the Prosecution produced a witness to testify about Karadjordjevo? What case is this? This is pure fiction. It has never been published anywhere. It has only been a matter of public speculation. It has never been put forward in any courtroom of this Tribunal, apart from speculative interpretations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, it's difficult for us to say, you know, something about this evidence, but we heard and we saw from the document many times on this kind of plan. I believe the Judges will arrive at correct conclusions on this issue. Should we not pursue on this issue any more and ask the Prosecution to continue. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All of you recognised, sir, including President Tudjman and you and Gojko Susak, all the persons in this meeting recognised that in order to accomplish this plan, as you told us a few minutes ago in your own words, when I did not interrupt you, this would require boundaries of municipalities to be redrawn and to be changed and for populations to be transferred. You all knew that, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew, and there was talk about the reorganisation of the then system of municipalities. This did not entail the transferral of populations, as the Prosecutor has just said, and this cannot be in this transcript. If it is in the transcript, then it certainly does not correspond to the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And also, you had indicated that when these three states were created, it would also be part of the concept that each of the ethnic states could have special ties, for instance, to some -- I will use the term "mother" or "parent state." The Croatian component of Bosnia-Herzegovina could have a special tie to Croatia, the Serb portion could have a special tie to Serbia, and I suppose the Muslims were a separate, different matter. And in fact, it was discussed that some of the sovereignty of these states might be transferred, to, for instance, Croatia, and that was discussed too, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was discussed, but only as a possibility, only conditionally. If this idea were to be implemented - and it was not - then the three states that might come into existence in Bosnia and Herzegovina might have special links, for example the Croatian state in Bosnia-Herzegovina with Croatia, the Serbian state with Serbia-Montenegro. The Muslim state might have ties with both or perhaps with a third country. But as this plan never actually came to life, then there is no point in discussing it before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to direct your attention to in the B/C/S version. It's page 8/5 to 8/6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for the others in the courtroom, it starts at the bottom of page 29. Mr. Usher, if you could help on the ELMO, if you could -- page 29, if you could put that part on the ELMO, please? If that could be -- and if you could move that up, please, just a bit, and if the video booth can assist us by zeroing in on the bottom part of the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this question in relation to this document because the witness stated that he never authorised this document, and even today we see that he has not read it. I think it would be fair for the witness to read the document and then to state what corresponds to the truth as he remembers it and what does not. And then it will be fair to put this question to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, I believe that is just a record of that meeting. The witness participated in that meeting himself and some words were quoted of what he said at that meeting. Yes, Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you then, in this part of the meeting, engaged in a conversation, specifically yourself along with Mr. Manolic, Mr. Koljevic, and starting on the bottom of page 29, you then stated your understanding of what Mr. Koljevic had said. "I understand Mr. Koljevic's proposal as follows: Three states would be established in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANOLIC
utterances.text: Three confederal states? Franjo Boras: Confederal, yes, with all the attributes of statehood. Nikola Koljevic: With a confederal agreement, yes. Franjo Boras: Yes, that's right, and that would be, among other things, the Croatian state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes. Whether it would be called that or something similar with probably two regions, two separate regions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BORAS
utterances.text: Two regions, two separate regions, because they could not be these geographic ones for various reasons, and now that Croatian state of Bosnia-Herzegovina includes a confederal agreement with the other two states of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Yes, with the Serbian and the Muslims because there are various things we have in common which we would include in that agreement because you cannot divide the sky. You cannot divide transport or road traffic, railway traffic, river traffic and so on. This means that we would have things on the basis of that confederal agreement which we would transfer to those joint institutions on the level of the confederation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and likewise the Croatian state of Bosnia-Herzegovina would transfer independently certain affairs of common interest with the Republic of Croatia, and we can even transfer unto the Republic of Croatia Foreign Affairs, those joint institutions of Foreign Affairs, Defence, even currency and so forth. That is how I proceed from this. Mr. President, we were already talking a bit about the concrete aspects of this proposal." That's what you said and that's the conversation on that part of the conversation at this meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely. I have already said that Mr. Koljevic was unable to explain his idea in an expert, professional manner. He was quite confused in his manner of presentation. He stated that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be preserved as a federal state consisting of three states, the Croatian state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Muslim state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Serbian state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as I said earlier, all three of these states could have close links with neighbouring countries, and if necessary, they could transfer parts of their sovereignty to either Croatia or Serbia-Montenegro, or in the case of the Muslim state, they need not do so, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to cut you off because of time. We only have a limited amount of time remaining. In fact, sir, you already had maps that had been drawn up about population and demographics, didn't you? And I refer to you page 13 of the English version and page 4/3 to 4/4 of the Bosnian-Croatian-Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Mr. Koljevic did not bring any maps with him on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't say that, sir. I didn't say you had the maps -- I didn't not say you had the maps in the room. You said this in the meeting: "We don't have an initial sketch. We have some maps which were drawn up now after the population census, on the basis of which, as you can see, that is the part that is primarily Croatian, that is" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: My apology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: "That is primarily Croatian. That is the part which is very compact and the easiest. Eastern Herzegovina, which is the easiest. We think, however, that this should be proceeded by a reorganisation of municipalities and referendums so that it could have a democratic shape. And this one, which could not -- and this one, which could not oppose it publicly, and we think that these processes could not be publicly halted. Manolic: The aim of that reorganisation would in fact be the homogeneity of certain areas." Now, that is what was discussed in the meeting, sir, wasn't it? And where did these maps come from, by the way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, what you have just read, I have not been able to follow in the Croatian language. These may be the words of Nikola Koljevic. I reiterate that the Croatian side, together with me, had no maps, no documents in connection with this idea that was brought to Zagreb by Mr. Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You had Mr. Anto Valenta's demographic maps, didn't you? In fact, the maps that you were talking about on page 13 here, were those Mr. Valenta's maps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you talked about how you would actually carry out these things and how the municipalities would be reformed and reshaped, and I direct your attention to the bottom of page 20 and in the Serbo-Croatian version, 6/3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in a democratic manner, through a referendum, which was permitted under the then constitution and is still permitted under the current constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said, sir: "In Interviso [phoen] again, we talked in the aeroplane about that today, having this problem in mind in particular and then we spoke, there, where there is a relative majority of Croats in the municipality and we need the additional votes of the Serbian people, then that municipality should be joined in its entirety to its Croatian entity. We could then carry out this in agreement, these two people, that we in turn help the Croatian people with our votes there where the Serbian people enjoy relative majority." Going to the top of page 21: "This does not arise as a problem with respect to the majority of municipalities, but it arises where -- there where a relative majority is held by one people and they need the help of another people. So that then that municipality as well would be joined to the Serbian or the Croatian entity. All this is with respect to the Muslim people. For example, in Mostar, in the municipality, on the basis of the new census, the Muslim people have prevailed over the Croatian people by 1 per cent. However, when the votes of the Serbian people are added to those of the Croatian people, then the municipality is" -- And then the Croatian Defence Minister Gojko Susak comes in: "Yes. That's similar to Travnik up there." That's what you discussed, isn't it? Lines that have to be redrawn, municipalities would have to be reformed, populations would have to be moved; true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not true. We discussed precisely those municipalities where the communist system had previously unfairly organised municipalities at the expense of the Croatian people or the Serbian people. I have already said - and I will say again - you, sir, are mentioning Mostar. Gojko Susak mentioned Travnik. This was where municipalities were unfairly organised. In Mostar a village was taken away from the Croats, Ljuti Dolac, and attached to Siroki Brijeg. It was detached from Mostar. Dreznica was removed from Jablanica and attached to Mostar. In this way, artificially, the Mostar municipality acquired a Muslim majority. The same was the case with Travnik and Kulen Vakuf in connection with the village of Dobretici. The situation was exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. And on page 21, sir, you agreed with Mr. Susak. You just told us what Mr. Susak said and you just said, in responding, continuing on page 21: "Boras: Yes." In responding to Susak: "Yes, it's similar to it. There are a large number of instances, yes. That could be resolved in this fashion, to proceed on the basis of agreement that great trust," et cetera. So indeed, you and Mr. Susak had that exchange, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this occasion, we talked about what is here, but we had never discussed it previously. Nor can it be concluded from this record that we were thinking of expelling a certain ethnic group from one territory and moving another one into the same territory. It can be concluded from the spirit of what is contained in these records that we wanted to carry this out in a democratic way, provided for by the constitution. Any municipality could be changed through a referendum, if the people of that municipality expressed their will through a referendum. That was what I meant then. I may not have expressed myself in the best way possible, in the way I would use now, but that was the spirit of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. -- President Tudjman -- and let's just go back to -- give me one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask the usher to put page 23 momentarily and -- I don't have that, counsel, and the witness. I apologise, I don't have that exact reference, but it should be somewhere shortly before 7 -- page 7/3. I apologise. I didn't make that notation in my notes. It's shortly before page 7/3. If you can put that on the ELMO? If it is -- now, about this time -- sorry, could we go down a little bit on the page? Where it says -- the other way, the other way, please. Sorry, and then about a bit up, that's good. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I put it to you, sir, the record reflects that this is about where President Tudjman enters the meeting. "Mr. President, we have already begun discussions. Mr. Koljevic set forth their views as a whole. We have started to clarify certain questions and problems a bit in our discussion. I think there is no controversy over what has been said as a whole. There probably will be when we proceed to specific issues." And then President Tudjman joins the conversation at that point, and he, President Tudjman himself, recognised, did he not, that what was being envisioned here would involve and require the movement, the exchange, the transfer of populations? Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember him saying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why don't you look, please, at Exhibit -- at page 7/3 and the bottom of page 25 in the English transcript? "The President: I don't know whether you -- from what I've heard already, the idea on national councils seems acceptable to me. In principle, such a principled agreement means that we should be forthcoming with respect to territorial delimitation, and that is acceptable because in this regard, history shows that not only was such understanding necessary but also population exchanges and so forth. The only thing I think is that this problem of confederal system is something that should be dealt with bearing in mind all the experiences to date."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not want to intervene before because I recognised that this is a very important document. However, I do not know where the Prosecutor is reading from. If this is the original, I will ask for an expert opinion on this translation, because if you will allow me let me read this in Croatian with your permission, of course. This is the Croatian original I received from the OTP. "I don't know whether, from what I have heard so far, comma, it seems acceptable to me, that is the idea of national councils, full stop. In principle, then, such principled agreement that one should be forthcoming in the sense of territorial delimitation, comma, and that is acceptable because history shows in this respect that sometimes it was necessary even, comma, not only such an understanding but sometimes even the exchange of populations and so on, full stop. I only think that the problem of a confederal system and so on and so forth." The President did not propose anything. He was simply giving explanations of things that had happened before in history. So in the Croatian version, there is no proposal in this sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, whether this is authentic or not, we could not know, because it's a matter of translation. I think there will be some experts in this Tribunal who will verify this paragraph. Shall we proceed with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I have only one more question about this document and then I have one last set of questions, and I'll be concluded, but I have one question about this document or one more passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, all of you knew as you sat in President Tudjman's office that day, on the 8th of February -- or excuse me, 8th of January, 1992, you all knew that the Muslims would never agree to this and that if they knew you were meeting about this, they would be very unhappy, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I direct you to the final -- my final question, Your Honour, on this transcript, page 35 in the English version, 10/1 in the Bosnian-Croatian version: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "Franjo Boras: I would add to your question, Mr. President, that the Muslims would not gladly accept this and that they would not be glad to hear of these discussion of ours this evening. Their concept, with Alija as the head, is a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina as civic state and by that very fact, as Professor Koljevic has already pointed out, they would like to ensure the preeminence of the Muslim people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the gradual eradication of the two peoples, especially the Croatian people, which is in minority there." You said that, didn't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct that I said that. I did say the Muslim side, with respect to the idea put forward by Mr. Koljevic, would not be pleased with it, because the idea of the Muslim side was a unitary Bosnia and Herzegovina, strictly centralised, without cantons, without provinces, without federal units, the units that emerged in various international plans. And among the delegations of the Serbian and Croatian side, we knew that, and I did say at that meeting that the Muslim side would not be happy with the discussions we were having in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, following this meeting, this is the proposal and the proposition that you began to promote and speak about publicly, didn't you, the separate states, the separate ethnic states?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You went on Serbian -- the former Yugoslavia -- the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia TV in early February 1992, and you said, essentially, in a very abbreviated sort of way, exactly -- talked about exactly the proposals that you talked about with President Tudjman on the 8th of January, 1992, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which television? I didn't understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was a Serbian broadcast by the television of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. You were being interviewed by a reporter and you told that reporter and said on public TV just what you have told us today: three ethnic states, three separate states, and if they wanted to, each of them could give a certain portion of their sovereignty to Croatia, on the one hand, or to Serbia, on the other. And that's what you said, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never did I take part in a public television programme of Serbia or Yugoslavia that you are referring to, never in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, as our final exhibit and question, I would ask the video booth to please play now for us Exhibit 898.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I'm not wrong in saying that the Defence was not given this videotape either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we've already made a ruling already, but for this witness, for this first witness, we'll let the Prosecution go, and we're eager to watch that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And I have a short transcription and translation. It's a very short clip. And I would add, Mr. President, the tape can be self-authenticating. The witness can say very clearly whether it's him shown in the videotape or not. Can we play the clip, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] In my opinion, a confederate state of Bosnia-Herzegovina should contain three federal units. Through those three federal units, all three peoples - the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims - would express their will. Within those federal units, they would have their own governing bodies, but at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a confederate state, they would have their joint bodies. In addition, each federal unit, especially the Serbian and the Croatian ones, would have the right to join, by means of an agreement, their home republics and to transfer to those home republics a part of their sovereignty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see myself on the screen. I see now, but not myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: For the booth, I suppose what's happening -- we'll have to play it again for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] In my opinion, the confederate state of Bosnia-Herzegovina should contain three federal units, the three peoples. That is to say, the Serbs, the Croats, and the Muslims would express their will through those three federal units. Within those federal units, they would have their own governing bodies, and at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as a confederal state, they would have their joint bodies. In addition, each federal unit, especially the Serbian and the Croatian ones, would be able, by means of an agreement, to link up with their home republics and to transfer a part of their sovereignty to those ethnic home republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, that is you in the videotape, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, only I couldn't conclude from this which television this is. But the text is okay. However, what I said and what is here on paper in front of me is quite a different political option of the internal set-up of Bosnia-Herzegovina in relation to what was discussed in Zagreb on the 8th of January, 1992. Actually, this is a political option of the Croatian Democratic Union before the elections. Even then, in our political platform, we stated that we wanted a confederal Bosnia-Herzegovina with three federal units: a Serbian, a Croatian, and a Muslim; that at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, institutions should be established that it is reasonable to have at the level of Bosnia-Herzegovina; and that these federal units, the Croatian and the Serbian, may have some close ties with their parent states, and even, if they so agree, to transfer their sovereignty to them. So this was our electoral platform, and it has nothing to do with the other one that Koljevic refers to, three states. Here we talk about three federal units. Over there, there was mention of three states. So this is something quite different as far as the internal state structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina is concerned. I stand by this, and this is the political platform of the Croatian people even before the elections, and it was on the basis of this platform that we won the elections. And this is in contradiction with the political platform of the Muslim people, or rather, the Party of Democratic Action, which wanted a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina without federal units. What Milosevic wanted at the level of Yugoslavia, and I'm saying again, one citizen, one vote, and we know what the reasons for that were. Alija Izetbegovic, through the programme of the party of SDA, wanted in Bosnia-Herzegovina the same thing. But I'm not sure that this was the Serbian or Yugoslav television, or it must be somewhere else, somewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or maybe even in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could, just three examples. I'll take three examples for the witness to respond briefly, for him to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 4/3 in the right-hand corner, top right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the agreement? It's been taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: No. It's Exhibit PT/3. I'm talking about the transcript, Exhibit PT/3, 4/3 in the top left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is in English.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could you please -- can you see the words "Boras Franjo"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Would you be kind enough to read that and tell us whether you said that or not, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [As read] "We had the idea that if we delineated territorially, then administratively it would not be possible to spread to Serbian and Croatian territories, because permission for construction would be obtained. They would be under the jurisdiction of those parts and settlement."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Only Koljevic could have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My question is: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Then read on, please. It says your name again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We don't have the first sketch. We have some maps which were made now after --"

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we have the English page references, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Is it possible to put the English version --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Page 12 in English. In English version, page 12. [Interpretation] Both quotations are on page 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: The second one, Franjo Boras.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [As read] "We don't have the first sketch. We don't have any maps that were made now after the population census, on the basis of which you see those are areas that are predominantly Croatian. Then there's this that is very compact and easiest, Eastern Herzegovina, which is the easiest. We think, however, that this should be preceded by a reorganisation of municipalities, and then referendums, so that it could have a democratic form, and this one, which could not oppose it publicly, and we think that these processes could not be publicly halted."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now my last question. Could you please put the map of the so-called banovina. I only have one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Did Bosnia-Herzegovina exist at that time in the kingdom of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I would just like to show -- put it on the ELMO. [Interpretation] I want to be fair to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: When the banovinas existed, did Bosnia and Herzegovina exist?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Just two questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, how many federal units has Bosnia-Herzegovina got today, or entities, as they are called?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: If the Bosniaks and the Croats were to delineate themselves, how many entities would we have then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have three entities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions from the Judges? Judge Clark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid to ask a couple of questions, because it might start a new debate. So if I could ask about three questions and everybody promises not to ask any questions arising out of what I ask. And if we can't make a deal on that, I'll keep quiet. Any agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So agreed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When it's you, Your Honour, I always agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm afraid I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, then you'll be the only one asking questions out of my re-examination

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Boras, when you ran for election first, at the very beginning of the democratisation of the former -- when the early democratisation process was beginning and you ran for election, did you run on the HDZ of Bosnia-Herzegovina ticket?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: With Mr. Kljuic as president?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: This was before any thought of the organisation or declaration of HZ HB. It would have been almost two years before -- one year before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So one year before.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- was when the democratic elections were held. One year, quite so. One year prior to the formation of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: At that time, was the platform for the HDZ the maintenance of the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina as they existed and recognition that there were three ethnic groups there who were entitled to equal respect and rights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When you took your oath of office, you and the six other members of the Presidency, to whom did you swear loyalty?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the constitution that was then in force, that we had inherited from the previous Communist authorities, that we would protect Bosnia-Herzegovina as a republic within the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. I have to say that this oath was subject of discussion for six hours. Why? Because democratic authorities were taking over, and now they have to take an oath that they will protect the Communist social order, which they inherited in practice and in the constitution. So a Solomonic solution was found for the text of the oath itself. So all parties that wants seats in parliament agreed to that oath, and as the members of the parliament took their oath according to that text, and so did we, as members of the Presidency. Although it was quite strange in our party programmes, our aim was to topple the Communist order which had been in power for 45 years in Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, throughout the then Yugoslavia. So it is quite true. We did take some sort of an oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It wasn't -- a short answer to this. Was the oath to preserve the integrity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, even though it was now a democratic institution but it was to preserve the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, even though it was now a democratic institution, but it was to preserve the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in its own boundaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible answer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. The next question I want to ask you, and probably the last: What exactly were your duties as a member of the Presidency? You tell us about how busy your duties -- how much your duties took you away from your home. What were your duties as a member of the Presidency before the war and during the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, and during the war as well, the duties of the Presidency, regular Presidency, was to conduct foreign affairs, or to be involved in foreign affairs; then the questions of defence, the defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; then appointment of diplomatic representatives abroad; giving approval and taking credentials from those coming to Bosnia-Herzegovina; and amnesty of convicted persons. So each member of the Presidency, as a collective body, acted through councils and commissions. There were two councils: the Council for Defence, which was headed by the president --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Was there any great difference between your duties when the War Presidency was in existence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were differences, because in the War Presidency, in addition to these duties that I have listed, we also had the legislative function, which earlier on was held by the Assembly. However, as it could not meet, these duties were transferred to us, and this was so stipulated by the constitution. That is, the War Presidency was able to pass decrees with the strength of law, but mainly in the aim of defending Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Boras.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Seric.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Her Honour has fully elaborated her questions, so that she has deprived me of the satisfaction of being able to ask some more questions myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, on behalf of the Bench, I would like to express our sincere thanks to you for your coming to The Hague to help us. All I would like to say is that we wish you a very pleasant flight, enjoyable holiday, and good health. The usher will show you out of the room.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.
